Component sheet · 13 sections

The whole surface of a town, drawn once.

Every specimen below is built from the published --ts-* token contract in packages/tokens. Not one hex literal appears in a section stylesheet, which is what lets a town reskin the shell and every resident-built creation inside it in the same move.

Mobile first: whole screens are drawn at 390 px inside a device, parts are drawn loose. Rationale sits beside the thing it explains.

01

Foundations and primitives

The atoms every other section is built from: the palette and what each colour is allowed to mean, the three voices of type, the 4px scale, and the controls a resident actually touches. Nothing here is decorative. If a token exists it is because something ships with it.

Surfaces The background is warm cream. White is a card lifting off it, not the page.
--ts-cream The screen. Every page sits on this. #f8f6f1
--ts-surface Cards and sheets. The only pure white in the system. #ffffff
--ts-stone Image placeholder and inert fill. Never text sits on it. #e5e1da
Ink and its alpha ramp One warm near-black at six opacities, stacked over cream so it reads as a ramp and not six greys.
--ts-ink100% Body text, headlines, anything you read.
--ts-ink6060% Secondary text: bylines, taglines, the lede.
--ts-ink4545% Eyebrows and metadata. Large or uppercase only.
--ts-ink2626% Disabled labels, dot separators, placeholder glyphs.
--ts-ink1313% Dividers and rules.
--ts-hairline11% Card borders. One notch quieter than a divider on purpose.
--ts-ink088% Shadow colour. Not a fill, never a border.
Muted text is ink at alpha, never navy at alpha. Navy is a brand colour, so a 60% navy secondary line drifts blue-cool against warm cream and quietly turns every byline into a link that is not one. Ink at 60% is the same hue as the headline above it, just further away, which is what "secondary" is supposed to look like. It also means one ramp survives a town reskin: when --ts-navy moves to green for the Delta theme, no body copy changes temperature. The inverse holds on dark cards, where the ramp becomes cream at alpha for the same reason.
Navy Structure and the one dark card per screen. It is a surface colour first, a text colour second.
--ts-navy Dark card fill, headers, the shell's own chrome. #26405b
--ts-navy-dark The deeper step, used when navy sits on navy. #22384e
--ts-navy80 Scrims and the navy shadow tint. 80%
--ts-navy60 Icon strokes inside navy-tinted areas. 60%
--ts-navy40 Borders on a navy tint. 40%
--ts-navy10 The tint itself: selected rows, quiet chips. 10%
Cream on navy-dark --ts-cream
Cream-muted, the secondary line on a dark card --ts-cream-muted
--ts-cream14
Accents Terracotta acts, gold announces, sage confirms, brick alarms. Four jobs, no overlap.
--ts-terracotta Primary action. The only colour that means "press this". #c4714e
--ts-terracotta-hover Pressed and hovered primary. One step darker, same hue. #b15f3b
--ts-terracotta-tint Opaque warm wash behind an active area. #fff3ec
--ts-terracotta10 Transparent wash that keeps whatever is under it. 10%
--ts-terracotta14 Creation icon tiles, quiet-button hover. 14%
--ts-gold Civic. City hall, notices, the thing the town posted. #e7ae2e
--ts-gold14 The notice card fill. 18% over cream. 18%
--ts-gold-text Text on gold. Raw gold is unreadable, this is the pair. #8a6510
--ts-sage Verified, open now, alive. Only when we actually know. #4c6b4b
--ts-sage-light Sage that survives being placed on navy. #86a585
--ts-sage14 Verified pill fill. 18%
--ts-brick Emergency only. Boil order, river crest, evacuation. #7e1f0c
Contrast, measured Real WCAG ratios for the pairs that ship. Two of them fail, and pretending otherwise would be worse than the failure.
PairSampleRatioBody 17pxLarge 21px+

--ts-ink60 on --ts-cream Lake Dardanelle 4.41 fails AA AA
--ts-ink45 on --ts-cream Lake Dardanelle 2.83 fails AA fails AA

--ts-cream on --ts-brick Lake Dardanelle 9.31 AAA AAA

Ratios computed against the composited colour, not the token's own value: an alpha ink over cream, gold-text over 18% gold over cream. The three that fail at body size have rules attached. --ts-ink45 is never allowed on body copy, only on 11px uppercase eyebrows and metadata where it is a label rather than a sentence, and it is never the only signal. --ts-ink60 at 4.41 misses AA by a hair at 17px, so secondary lines that carry real information (a byline, an address) are set at --ts-ink and only truly ancillary ones use it. --ts-terracotta is a fill colour, not a text colour: on a primary button it carries --ts-surface at 3.61, which passes only at large sizes, so the button label is 15px semibold and gets the same treatment large text does. Terracotta as small body text is banned.

Between the steps, bare px is fine and deliberate: the shipped shell uses 13.5px for a dense list row and 14.5px for a tight card subtitle. A scale that forbids the half step just gets ignored.

Measure Newsreader at 17px, 1.6 line height, capped at 66ch. Past about 75 characters the eye loses the return.

The Pope County Quorum Court will take up the Marina Way rezoning again on Tuesday, after a first vote in June stalled on a question nobody in the room could answer: whether the old ferry landing parcel is inside the flood easement or beside it. The county surveyor says the maps disagree with each other and have since 1978.

Public comment opens at 6pm at the courthouse on West Main. If you plan to speak, you sign in at the door and you get three minutes, which is not long, so people tend to write it down first.

Radius, on the shapes that use it Radius is proportional to the thing. A 10px corner on a 16px chip looks broken, which is why chips are round instead.

The button radius is 10px and not a pill. Chips are pills because a pill reads as removable, filterable, transient: it is a token you can pick up and put down. A button is a commitment, and it should look like it has edges. The practical version of the argument is that Town Square puts buttons next to inputs constantly, and an input cannot be a pill without its text drifting off the optical centre at either end. Matching --ts-radius-button to --ts-radius-input at 10px means a search field and its adjacent Go button share a silhouette instead of arguing. 10px is also the point where a 44px-tall control still reads as a rectangle rather than a lozenge, which keeps the pill meaning available for chips, where we actually need it.
Elevation Five steps and each one names a distance from the page, not a mood. Shadows are ink at 8%, never black.
--ts-shadow-flat

A card resting on the page. Directory rows, article rows, anything in a list.

--ts-shadow-raised

The hover state of a flat card, and the resting state of anything tappable that stands alone.

--ts-shadow-lifted

A card that has been picked up: dragged, expanded, or the lead story at the top of Today.

--ts-shadow-overlay

Sheets, dialogs, menus. Anything with a scrim behind it. The only step with a long, soft second layer.

--ts-shadow-navy

Reserved for the dark card. A neutral shadow under navy reads grey and dirty, so this one tints with the card.

Button variants and sizes Four intents, three sizes. Every size clears 44px of touch target even when the box is 34px tall.
Small · 34px

Brick is never a delete button, so destructive is outlined terracotta. --ts-brick is the single alarm register in this system. It appears when the water plant issues a boil order and when the river is forecast over the levee, and its whole value is that a resident has almost never seen it before. Spend it on "remove creation" and you have taught the town that the loudest colour in the app means a form did something, which is exactly the training you do not want at 6am in a flood. So destructive borrows terracotta but changes shape rather than hue: transparent fill, a full-weight terracotta border, terracotta label. It is unmistakably not the primary button standing beside it, it still reads as consequential, and it costs the palette nothing. Confirmation of a genuinely irreversible action is the dialog's job, not the button's colour.
Every state, rendered at once Static [data-state] specimens so the whole matrix is visible, and the same rules drive the live pseudo-classes. Hover one and it behaves.

Loading keeps the label and swaps the leading slot for the spinner, so the button does not resize under the finger that just pressed it. It sets aria-busy and stays disabled, because a second press would submit a second vouch.

Icon and width variants An icon-only button always carries an aria-label. There is no such thing as an obvious glyph.
Filter chips The count is inside the chip because a filter with no results should say so before you press it.
Status pills Every pill carries a glyph as well as a colour, so the state survives being printed, dimmed, or read by someone who cannot separate sage from stone.
Open now Verified From city hall Live now Draft Pending review Emergency

Only the last one is brick, and in a normal week it is not rendered at all. "Pending review" is ink on stone rather than amber, because waiting for the committee is not a warning.

The focus ring on three backgrounds A 2px halo in the page colour then 2px of terracotta, so the ring never fuses with what is behind it.
on cream
on surface
on navy

The cream halo does its real work on navy, where it separates the terracotta ring from a dark field it would otherwise sit too close to. On white the halo is nearly invisible, which is fine: the terracotta ring is carrying it there. Focus is only ever drawn on :focus-visible, so a mouse press does not leave a ring behind.

02

Navigation and shell

How a resident moves through the town, and how the shell frames everything else. The bar names the place, the bottom nav names the five things you can do, and every surface between them is a variation on one idea: say where you are, then get out of the way.

Resident bar, four identity states The ring is the badge. A separate tick would be one more thing on a bar that already carries the mark.

Four of ten vouches. No ring, and the account sheet is where the count lives. The bar does not nag.

Verified never means publicly identified. The ring says neighbours vouched, and says nothing about who you are.

Unread notification
Town Square
Russellville, Arkansas

A dot, not a count. Three notifications and thirty feel the same at a glance, and the number is a small anxiety with no payoff.

The bar carries four things and refuses a fifth: who made this (the mark), where you are (the place line), find something, and you. Every product like this eventually grows a hamburger, and the hamburger is where the five destinations go to die. They are at the bottom, under a thumb, instead.

Bar at rest and condensed on scroll The place line is an orientation, not a label. Once you are reading you already know what town you are in.

Three bars, one set of class names, zero markup differences. The only thing that changed is a data-town attribute on an ancestor, which reassigns values behind the same token names. That is the seam the whole platform is built on: a resident in Helena gets their own town, and a creation someone shipped in Russellville styled with var(--ts-navy) comes along intact. If any of these three needed a component change, the second town would fork the first and the third would never happen.

Bottom navigation, state matrix Active carries a rule, a weight and aria-current. Colour is the fourth signal, never the only one.

Disabled stays focusable and keeps its label. A greyed target you cannot tab to is a dead end with no explanation, so tapping it opens sign in.

Pressed and keyboard focus
Today Nearby Calendar Creations You

Five destinations, and the fifth is the argument. Creations sits in the nav as a peer, not under a More menu, because the thesis is that value compounds with builders. A platform that hides the thing residents made has already decided it is a news app. Everything else a builder needs lives off the You tab and the command palette, so the resident path stays five words wide.

Safe area and target size The home indicator is not a design element you can borrow. Padding, not margin, so the fill runs to the glass.
Today Nearby Calendar Creations You env(safe-area-inset-bottom)
Target
48 × 56, never under 44 × 44. The label is inside the target, so the tap area is the whole column and not the 20px glyph.
Inset
padding-bottom: calc(var(--ts-space-2) + env(safe-area-inset-bottom)). Padding keeps the cream fill running under the home indicator; a margin would leave a stripe of page showing through.
Reach
Bottom edge on purpose. The five things a resident does live under the thumb, and the two things the app wants (search, account) are the stretch.
Keyboard
The bar is position: sticky, not fixed, so an open keyboard pushes it off screen instead of pinning it over the field being typed into.

Today is 640px of reading column and nothing else, centred against a 220px rail, with the peripheral things in a third column that a resident can ignore forever without missing anything. The obvious move at this width is a dashboard of cards, and it is the wrong one: a dashboard implies everything is equally urgent, which is exactly the Nextdoor feeling we are avoiding. Nearby is different and gets the wide grid, because browsing 700 businesses is a scan rather than a read, and a scan wants many things in the eye at once. The test is what the column is for, not how much room the window happens to have.

Desktop shell at 1200px, Nearby Same rail, same bar, no reading cap. Browsing wants breadth; the aside is gone because the grid is the content.

The host header is the seam a resident can feel. It is the one header set on navy, it names the neighbour who built the thing, and it says out loud what the sandbox can see. A creation that looked exactly like the rest of the app would be more elegant and much worse: the whole trust model depends on a resident knowing when they have stepped into something a neighbour wrote. The close control is a cross, not a chevron, because you are leaving rather than going back.

Tabs, segmented control, chip rail Three shapes for three jobs: peer views, one view filtered, and a list too long to fit.
Underline tabs — peer views, each a different set of things

Underline plus aria-selected plus a weight change. Counts sit in the tab because "128 articles" is a reason to press it.

Segmented control — one view, filtered

A pill, never an underline. Underline means "you are somewhere else now"; a pill means "the same list, fewer of them".

Chip rail — the long category list, scrollable

The rail bleeds to the right edge and a fade sits over the last 32px, which is the only honest way to say "there is more". A chip that ends flush with the margin reads as the end of the list.

Search, resting and expanded One field over five kinds of thing. A resident looking for Riverfest does not know whether it is a story or an event.

Grouped
Five groups, each with its own leading icon, because the icon is what lets a resident skip four groups without reading them. A single ranked list mixes a business with a neighbour and makes both harder to find.
Capped
Two rows per group and a see-all row. The overlay is for recognising the thing you already had in mind, not for exhausting the index.
Order
Groups sort by best match, not by a fixed hierarchy. Search "Riverfest" in July and Events comes first; search it in November and Stories does.
Privacy
People match on handle only. There is no address to search on and there never will be, so the field cannot become a lookup tool for finding a neighbour.
Search with nothing to show An empty field is a chance to teach the index. A dead end should hand you the next thing to try.

The no-results screen is the one that decides whether a directory grows. "No results found" is a full stop; two near misses and an add button is an invitation, and the person who just searched for the missing thing is the single best-qualified person in town to fill the gap. The 700 businesses we start with came from a scrape. The ones that make it worth opening in year two come from this screen.

180px. One decision and a way out. The scrim stays light because the page behind is still the thing you are looking at.

Back, and where a breadcrumb earns its place Back is a history. A breadcrumb is a claim about structure, and most screens do not have one.
A story — back only

The label names where you will land, not the word "Back". A resident who arrived from a shared link gets "Today" here too, because that is where the control actually goes.

A directory category, three levels deep — breadcrumb
Nearby Home services Roofing

Nine roofers is a leaf on a tree with 700 leaves. The crumb is how a resident gets back up one level to the other home services rather than out to Nearby and in again.

Collapsed on a narrow screen
Nearby Roofing

First and last survive, the middle collapses to a control that expands. Truncating the last crumb would hide the one thing the resident is looking at.

Today, Calendar, Creations and You get no breadcrumb at all. They are flat, and a crumb reading "Today › Dardanelle lock reopens" invents a hierarchy to describe a tap. The directory is the only genuinely nested thing in the product, so it is the only place that earns one.

The key handler only binds when the session holds a builder scope. Not hidden with CSS, not rendered and disabled: absent.

Keyboard only. There is no button for it anywhere in the resident shell, because a button is how a builder surface starts leaking into the town.

Two audiences, one app, and this is where that promise is actually kept. A resident who never writes a line of code should be able to use Town Square for a year and never encounter a manifest, a review queue or an MCP token. The separation is enforced by what mounts, not by what is styled quietly, and the visual distance is a second line of defence so that a builder screenshot is never mistaken for the resident product.

Footer, sign-off and the timestamp The timestamp is not decoration. It is the only way a resident can tell a quiet failure from a quiet day.

When a scrape fails, the API serves the last good screen rather than an error, which is right: a resident opening this at 6am wants the town, not a stack trace. But that policy quietly turns every failure into a lie unless something on the page says how old the answer is. The stale line is gold, not brick. Brick is the one alarm register and it is reserved for an actual emergency, which a late calendar scrape is not. Spending it here is how it stops meaning anything the morning the river is up.

A sheet or the omni overlay traps focus and returns it to the control that opened it. Escape closes, every time, everywhere.

03

News, the feed, and the reader

Town Square aggregates a handful of real sources and links out to every one of them. We never host the article. That single constraint decides the lead, the row, the cluster and the reader page: our job is to be the fastest honest route to somebody else's reporting, and to be legible on the mornings when the town published nothing at all.

The lead, four ways The town does not reliably ship art, so art is never the layout. Four heroes, one picked by what the story actually has.
News

The four are a ladder, resolved in one pass: developing outranks everything if a story is still moving, then photograph if the source shipped art, then pull-quote if an editor marked a line, then typographic. Nothing else competes for the slot. The reason there is no fifth variant with a grey box in it is that a broken image at the top of the town's front page reads as a broken town, and we would rather change the layout than show the hole. The live marker is a pip and the word Developing together, never the pip alone.

The cluster Three sources on one vote currently look like three stories. Clustered, the duplication becomes the value: who covered it, in what medium, how fast.
3 sources covering

The council rezoned the Weir Road corner for apartments on Tuesday night, 4 to 1.

That sentence is ours. Every headline below belongs to the newsroom that wrote it.

4 updates since Friday

This is the pattern local aggregation gets wrong most often, and the failure is always the same: three rows, three headlines, one event, and a reader who concludes the feed repeats itself. Collapsing to a single row and picking a winner is worse. It hides that the radio station has the tape and the blogger was in the room, and it quietly ranks a daily paper above a person writing on her own, which is exactly the judgement an aggregator has no standing to make. So the cluster keeps every source, at the same size, ordered by time and nothing else. Our one sentence at the top is the event, written plainly and labelled as ours, because passing a synthesised headline off as a publisher's is the fastest way to lose the sources we depend on. The medium tag matters more than it looks: Reported, Audio and Opinion let a reader pick what they actually want in about a second, and it is the one piece of editorial judgement we can make without stepping on anyone.

The Courier and The Dardanelle Post share navy on purpose, and the sheet shows the collision rather than hiding it: with five tints and a town that will keep adding sources, a unique colour per source was always going to run out, and a system that quietly degrades is better than one that breaks. The tile is a recognition aid at a glance. The name underneath it is the identification, and it is always present, which is also why the tile is aria-hidden.

The skeleton is drawn from the same rules as the feed, not from a generic set of grey bars: the lead art is 200px because the lead art is 200px, the third row has no thumbnail because roughly half of stories have none, and the section labels are real text, immediately because we always know what the sections are before we know what is in them. A skeleton that does not match its own screen produces a visible jolt on every load, and the jolt is what teaches people the app is slow. Open, drawn loose. It is a <details>, closed by default, and it works with the sheet's script disabled.

This page has to be useful to a reader and respectful of a publisher in the same breath, and those two pull in opposite directions: everything that makes it a better read makes it a better substitute for the article. The resolution is a hard ceiling. Three sentences and three points, never more, set in a panel that is visibly ours and labelled Town Square summary, with the line underneath saying plainly that we have nothing The Courier does not. The photograph runs at thumbnail scale with a credit and a link, not full bleed. The only prominent control on the screen is the one that leaves. A reader who wants the story goes and gets it from the people who did the work, and the summary is enough to decide whether to spend the click, which is the actual job.

Why am I seeing this is on every story, not buried in settings, because the honest answer is short and it is the answer people assume they will not get. Newest first inside the topics you chose. No profile, no engagement score, no paid placement. Writing it down where a resident meets it costs a disclosure and buys the only thing an aggregator has, which is being believed.

A developing story, collapsed and open A story that accretes over four days is four rows in a feed and one thing in a resident's head. The timeline matches the head.

Collapsed. The default in the feed. The newest entry is visible without opening anything, because that is what a returning reader came for.

  3. Sat1 Aug Neighbours filed a petition with 214 signatures against the change. PC Pope County Notebook morning

You will get one notice when this moves, not one per source.

Open. Newest at the top, oldest at the bottom, the date rail carrying the shape. Each entry is one sentence of what changed and a link to who said so.

The rule that makes this work is that every entry is one sentence about what changed, not a headline. Headlines stacked in date order are just the feed again with a border round it. "The city posted Tuesday's agenda, the rezoning is item 9" is the thing a resident following this actually needs, and it is a sentence we can write honestly from a public document without touching anyone's copy. The following state promises one notice per move, not one per source, which is the difference between a thread that is worth following and three notifications about the same vote.

Pull-quote and stat callout The serif voice doing editorial work. Both carry an attribution, because a number without a source is a rumour.

Quiet, not shouty. It sits inside a reader page or a topic header and never opens a feed on its own.

The figure is serif and large, the unit is small beside it, and the attribution is a link. A stat we cannot source does not get drawn.

Save, in every state it has Saving is optimistic and offline is normal, so the interesting state is the failure, and it holds the story rather than dropping it.

Four states, one control, one position. The failure keeps the story in a local queue and says so in words a person can act on. It is terracotta, not the alarm register: a save that has not landed yet is not an emergency.

A town with nothing to report is the normal case, not the error case, and the difference between those two framings is the whole tone of the product. The quiet day screen never apologises and never pads. It says what is true, it says why that is fine, and then it does the one genuinely useful thing available, which is offering yesterday in a compact list for somebody who was busy. What it does not do is invent a section. A screen that fills itself out on a slow Wednesday teaches people it was padded on the Wednesday the river came up, and that is a lesson a town information service does not get to unteach.

Relative time, the whole rule set We count minutes for exactly one hour, then switch to the words a neighbour would use. Nobody says "seven hours ago" out loud.
Age Renders as Why
Under a minute just now A number this small is noise. It means the page you are looking at is current.
1 to 59 minutes 18 minutes ago The only place we count, and the only timestamp allowed to go dark and bold. Inside an hour, the number changes what a resident does next.
Same day, over an hour this morning Also this afternoon and tonight, cut at noon and 6pm. Everyone knows what this morning means without doing arithmetic against their own watch.
Yesterday yesterday afternoon Keeps the part of day, because "yesterday afternoon" and "yesterday, 11:04 pm" answer different questions about a council vote.
2 to 6 days Tuesday A weekday name inside the last week is unambiguous and it is what people say. No "4 days ago".
7 days to a year 3 Jun Past a week the relative form stops helping. This is a date, and it is short enough to sit in a byline.
Over a year 3 Jun 2025 The year appears only when it is doing work, which is the moment a saved story could be mistaken for a current one.
Anything developing updated 12 minutes ago A live story keeps the minute count past the hour and takes the word updated, because on a developing story the question is not when it started, it is when it last moved.
On a scheduled item Monday, 6pm Anything in the future is an absolute time, always. A meeting "in 3 days" is how somebody misses a meeting.

Every timestamp in the section is serif and sits in the byline, never in a chip and never in mono. The rule set exists because inconsistent time is the fastest way for an aggregator to feel untrustworthy: a feed showing 2 hours ago beside Tuesday beside 08/04 tells a reader the screen was assembled by three different people who never met. One ladder, one voice, and the full timestamp is always on the element's title and in the reader page byline for anyone who needs the real number.

04

Events, the calendar, and what’s on this weekend

Everything here is scraped from the city, Arkansas Tech, the Pope County Library, half a dozen churches, the Center for the Arts and the parks department. The data is messy by nature: missing end times, a postal address where a venue name should be, things that recur, things that get cancelled at four in the afternoon. These components are designed against that reality rather than against a clean seed dataset.

The four category tints already ship and they are tokens, not shades picked to look nice beside the last one: civic is gold, music is sage, sport is terracotta, community is navy. Everything below extends that vocabulary rather than adding to it. The fifth state is the honest one, an event the categoriser would not confidently place, and it gets no colour at all.

Three things carry it, and none of them is colour alone. The clock is hatched over, because the clock is the promise that broke. The category tint is withdrawn to inert stone, because a tint is a claim that something is happening. The venue line is replaced by who cancelled it and when. The title stays full weight and full black.

Cancellation is the most common correction in the feed, so it cannot use brick. Brick is the one alarm register and spending it on a rained-out market is how it stops meaning anything at 6am when the river is up. Withdrawal reads as loudly as alarm here and costs nothing.

Why it resolves this way

The now line is a list item, not an overlay. It sits between two rows in document order, so it is announced in reading order and never lands on top of a title. It carries a real clock time because “now” on a screen someone left open for an hour is a lie.

The gap is written, not drawn. Four hours of nothing on a civic calendar is normal and should feel normal. A dotted line with “3 hr” on it reads as an error; a sentence reads as a town.

Earlier today collapses, it does not disappear. Three events that already happened are still the answer to “did I miss it”, which is a question people ask this screen constantly.

Tomorrow is on the same scroll. At nine in the evening, today is over and the honest answer to “what’s on” is tomorrow morning. A day view that dead ends at midnight makes the user navigate to learn nothing.

The week strip density as dots, because a number in a 44px cell is a number nobody reads
one a few a lot, the bar means four or more – nothing on

Every cell is a button, 52px wide and 68 tall, comfortably past the 44px floor, and every one carries an aria-label with the real count because dots are a glance affordance and not an accessible one. Today is a terracotta ring; selected is a navy fill. Both at once is the common case, so they have to compose: the ring survives inside the fill. A day with nothing on gets an en dash rather than an empty space, because empty space reads as “not loaded yet”.

The one written line

The lede is set in Newsreader at 15.5px, the only editorial voice on the screen, and it is the single element on this whole surface that a person writes. Everything below it is scraped.

It is worth the effort because it is the difference between a digest and a dump. “Move in weekend at Tech, so the whole town is busier than it wants to be” is a thing a neighbour says. No aggregator generates that, and a resident can tell within one sentence which one they are reading.

Saturday gets a card, Friday and Sunday get rows. The weekend has one obvious marquee thing and ten ordinary ones, and flattening that into eleven identical cards throws away the only editorial judgement in the product.

Counts are on the day heading, so a light Sunday is stated rather than implied by a short list, which could equally mean the scrape failed.

Event detail plain words first, exact times second; both notices sit above the fold because they change whether you go

Why it resolves this way

Plain words first. “Saturday morning, this weekend” is the answer to the question actually being asked. The exact stamp sits directly under it for the person who is putting it in a calendar, and neither has to be hunted for.

The moved notice is above the when, not below it. It is gold, the civic and notices register, and it says what changed and where it changed from. A resident who drove to Depot Park last August needs the old location named, not a corrected address with no history.

Recurrence is stated twice on purpose: once as a chip beside the category, once as a date bounded sentence. “Every Saturday” with no end date is how a calendar quietly fills with things that stopped happening in October.

The source line is not a footnote. Everything on this screen came from somebody else’s website, and saying so, with the time we last looked, is the whole basis for trusting the rest of it.

The category system, and the fifth state four tints and an honest blank; a wrong category is worse than no category
Civic Gold. Council, commissions, quorum court, public hearings, elections. city council · commission · public hearing · quorum court
Music Sage. Concerts, the Center for the Arts season, open mic, choir. concert · live music · open mic · recital · choir
Sport Terracotta. Tech home games, rec league, 5Ks, the river rides. vs. · tournament · 5k · scrimmage · playoff
Community Navy. The honest default. Market, story time, church suppers, everything else that is plainly a gathering. the fallback when nothing else matched
Not categorised No tint. A ring instead of a fill. The categoriser had a title it could not place and we did not guess. “July/August summer session ends”

An early build of the categoriser matched a bare session, which tinted “July/August summer session ends” gold as a council meeting. A category that is wrong is worse than no category: the tint exists so a resident can skip what they do not care about, and one that misfires teaches them to stop trusting all four. So the API stays deliberately narrow and the interface has to have somewhere honest to put the leftovers. That is the ring: same 34px tile, same position, no fill, no colour claimed. It reads as unlabelled rather than as other, which is the truth. Colour is never the only carrier either, every tile has its own icon and every list row has words.

If it is open to the town, it belongs here. Four boxes, and you can be rough with the date, we will work it out.

Type it however you say it. “Saturday morning” and “8/22 at 7” both work.

A neighbour reads this before it goes up

Usually within a day. We check it is real and it is open to everyone, we do not edit what you wrote. You will get a note either way.

Posting as @dardanelle_dave, verified. Your handle shows on the listing, nothing else does.

Why it resolves this way

Four fields and one of them is optional. Every field past this point is a field that stops somebody submitting a fish fry. Category, cost, end time and description are all things we can infer, ask later, or live without.

The date field takes prose. A structured date picker is the single most abandoned control in a form like this on a phone. Parsing “next fri 6ish” and then showing our work is strictly better than making a resident operate a calendar widget.

The review notice is a promise, not a warning. It says who reads it, roughly when, and explicitly that we will not rewrite their words. Moderation that is not described in advance reads as censorship when it happens.

Identity stays pseudonymous. Verified means neighbours vouched for them, not that the town knows where they live. The listing shows the handle and the badge, and nothing else exists to show.

We cleaned this up for you, and the submitted state show the parse and let them reject it; a silent correction is a bug the resident finds on the night
Confirm the parse

next fri 6ish

We read that as

Friday 14 August, 6:00 pm

No end time, which is fine. We will show it as running on.
Sent

It’s in the queue

Boat Club fish fry, Friday 14 August at 6:00 pm, Lake Dardanelle State Park.

Someone usually gets to these inside a day. We will let you know when it goes up.

Ambiguous parse
You typed

the 12th, evening

Two ways to read this
And roughly what time in the evening?

The parser will be right most of the time and catastrophically wrong occasionally, and the failure mode is a family showing up to a pavilion on the wrong Friday. So it never applies a correction silently. It shows the words the resident typed, immediately above what it made of them, and gives an equally weighted way to reject it. When it is genuinely ambiguous, it does not pick a winner and hope, it asks, which takes one tap and removes the entire class of problem.

RSVP, and the honest version when it is not ours we do not run somebody else’s door list, so we do not draw a control that implies we do

A scraped event is somebody else’s event. Drawing a Going button on the library’s book sale, collecting taps, and sending them nowhere is a fake capability, and it costs exactly one disappointed resident at a door to burn the trust the whole product runs on. So the link out state has no segmented control at all, it explains in a sentence why, and it offers the one thing we can honestly do, which is remember it for you. The zero state names its own age too: “nobody has answered yet” beside a listing posted three weeks ago says something quite different.

Reminders, with the thing it will actually send showing the notification at the moment of choosing is the only way to know if you want it

The second one is the only notification we send without being asked, and only to people who set a reminder for the thing that got cancelled.

A reminder toggle with no preview is a request to imagine a notification, and people imagine the annoying version and leave it off. Drawing it here also forces the copy to be worth an interruption: the time, the place, and one fact that changes whether you get in the car. The weather line is in there because at seven in the morning in August in the river valley it genuinely is the deciding factor.

The skeleton is the agenda row’s own geometry: 46px gutter, 34px tile, two lines. Nothing reflows when the data lands.

These three are the same screen with no events on it, and the resident has to be able to tell them apart in under a second. Quiet is warm and names something else to do. Broken says which source failed, when we last had good data, what to do instead, and leaves the stale rows visible and marked rather than hiding them. Loading holds the exact shape of what is coming. The failure state gets gold and not brick: a city calendar timing out is a notice, not an emergency, and brick has to still mean something at 6am when the river is up.

The directory and discovery

Seven hundred and forty one real Russellville listings, plus the town's articles and podcasts. This is built for stumbling onto a place you did not know to look for. Search exists, but it is the fallback, not the product. Everything here obeys one honesty rule: we only assert a business is open when we actually parsed its hours.

Looking for something specific?

Everything above the fold answers "show me something". The random draw sits first because it is the only control that requires no vocabulary at all. Then open right now, which is the one thing on the screen with a deadline attached to it and therefore the most likely to turn into a trip. Then the deliberate browse, then the curated collections, and only then a search field, set as a quiet outline button under a heading that names it as the exception. A search box in the header would tell every arriving resident that the correct way to use this is to already know the answer, which is exactly the behaviour the directory is supposed to replace.

The intro is set in the serif and says a true, specific number. It is the only place on the screen where the product speaks in its own voice, and it is doing a job: 741 and you have been to thirty reframes the directory as a place with a lot left in it rather than a lookup table you have already exhausted.

The stumble surface a card you flip, not a lever you pull: no spin, no reveal delay, no counter climbing

Hours not confirmed

Nothing is being scored and nothing is being saved unless you save it.

A slot machine withholds. It spins, it delays, it implies you might win. This does the opposite: the next card is already there, visible as two edges behind the current one, and the swap is a 160 ms cross of opacity and a 0.6 deg rotation, the physical feeling of a card being turned over on a table. There is no counter climbing, no streak, no "you've seen 12 today". The footer says plainly that nothing is being scored, because the moment this surface starts keeping score it becomes a game about the app rather than a way to find a bike shop.

Two actions, weighted. Show me another is the primary because the honest expectation is that most draws are a miss, and a miss should cost one tap. Seeing the full listing is the quieter button, which is the correct ranking: stumbling is cheap, committing is deliberate.

The open-now system unknown is the load-bearing state: 184 of our 741 listings have no hours we could read
Open until 9 PM Solid dot, sage. We parsed a full week and the clock is inside it.
Closes in 40 minutes Dot with a halo, gold. Fires inside the last hour, never earlier.
Opens 10 AM today Half dot. Closed right now but the same day is still in play.
Closed, opens 7 AM Thursday Hollow dot, ink. Always names the next opening, never just "Closed".
Tue to Sat, hours vary No dot at all. A clock and the raw string exactly as we hold it.
Hours not confirmed And when there is no string either, we say that instead of guessing.
Why no dot for unknown A grey dot beside a green dot reads as "closed". Unknown is not closed, it is us not knowing, and those two facts must not share a shape. Dropping the dot and swapping in a clock changes the glyph, not just the colour.
Colour is never alone Four distinct dot shapes, one icon substitution, and a text string that states the fact in words. Desaturate the whole sheet and every state is still readable.
The rule in one line openNow is nullable. Null renders the clock branch. Nothing downstream is allowed to coerce null to false.

What we know, and where it came from

  • Name, address, phone from the public Google Places listing, read on 10 December 2025.
  • Hours from the same listing. A full week was published, so we parse them and we are willing to say "open".
  • The description was written by a resident, @marcusd, and edited twice. See the 3 versions.
  • Photos are not ours. Nobody has added one yet. Add a photo.

Is this your business?

Claim the listing and you can fix the hours, add photos, and say what you actually do. Verification is a phone call to the number above, not a form.

Something here is wrong Edit history

Three actions, three targets, three destinations. Call opens the dialler, directions hands off to Maps, website leaves for a browser. Rolling them into one tappable card would make "read the menu" and "start driving" the same gesture, which is the exact mistake the shipped directory card already avoids. Each one names where it goes underneath the verb, so nobody taps Website expecting a phone number.

The provenance block is the part that makes this directory trustworthy rather than merely populated. It says the source, the date, and who touched it, and it is honest that we have no photographs instead of quietly drawing a stock image of some other town's bookshop. It also doubles as the contribution invitation: every line that admits a gap ends in a link that closes it.

Claimed is a provenance change, not a promotion. The listing does not rise in any ranking, get a bigger card, or lose the correction link. All that changes is the source line: these facts now come from the person who unlocks the door in the morning. A verified badge that also bought better placement would make the badge worthless as information, and would turn a town directory into an ad product.

The note on the map is not decoration. A map that fetches tiles is the first thing in this app to talk to a server that is not ours, and in a product built on not tracking anyone that is a decision with a name attached, declared in the manifest, not a library someone dropped in.

The matched substring is marked in every row, which is the cheapest possible way to answer why is this here. Without it, "Farmers Cooperative" under the query "coop" looks like a fuzzy-match accident rather than an exact one. Groups are labelled and ordered places, podcasts, articles, collections, because a person typing four letters into a town directory is looking for a place far more often than an episode, and a single mixed ranking would bury that.

Search is deliberately plain. No recent searches, no trending queries, no suggested terms. Every one of those would be a small surveillance surface, and the product does not need them: the answer to "I do not know what to type" is the stumble button, not a list of what other people typed.

The correction path is six taps and no typing, because the person who notices that Las Palmas closed is standing outside it in the rain. Adding a place asks for two fields, and the hours field explicitly invites you to leave it empty. That is the honesty rule pushed all the way up into the input: an empty hours field produces a truthful unknown state, and a well-meaning guess produces a green dot that sends someone across town for nothing.

Loading, empty and stale the stale notice reports a fact about us, not an accusation about the business
Loading the browse grid

The skeleton holds the exact geometry of the browse card, including the 16:10 photo box, so nothing jumps when the real data lands. Screen readers get a live "loading 86 places" instead of nine empty boxes.

A category with nothing in it yet

No pet groomers in the directory yet

There are at least two in town. We have not got them written down, which is a gap in our records and not a fact about Russellville.

Stale listing notice

We have not been able to reach this business's site since March.

The listing is still here because the phone number worked the last time somebody tried it. That is all we know. It may have closed, it may have changed hands, or the website may simply be gone.

Gold, not brick. Brick is the one alarm register in this system and it is reserved for the river coming up, not for a dead domain. The wording is deliberately about our reach rather than the business's status, because "we could not load their website" and "they went under" are wildly different claims and only one of them is ours to make in public about a neighbour's livelihood.

06

Creations

The build layer: small apps residents make and ship into Town Square. Each one is a static bundle running in a sandboxed iframe on a different domain, talking to the shell through a postMessage SDK and inheriting the town's design tokens. This section covers the gallery, the cards, the seam between our chrome and their code, the trust sheet, write-back consent, failure, and the invitation to build one.

A gallery of resident-built apps has one job that an app store does not have: it has to make the person scrolling it think I could build one of these. So it is not arranged by popularity and it does not lead with icons. It leads with a story about a person, because the gap a resident is actually trying to cross is not technical, it is permissional. Marta is a library clerk. If Marta did it, the thought goes, the door is open. Everything else on the screen is downstream of that: every card carries a human name in the same weight as the app name, the counts are neighbors who used it rather than downloads, and the build invitation is a quiet permanent fixture rather than a banner that appears once. An app store sells you things other people made. This is a town noticeboard for things your neighbors made, and the difference has to be visible in three seconds.

Build one

Describe what you want to the AI tool you already use, connect it to Town Square, and a neighbor on the review committee reads it before it goes up. Most of these took a weekend.

Nobody is paid for anything on this page. The source of every creation is public and you can fork any of them.

What the gallery refuses to be

Not an app store. No stars, no five-across icon grid, no ranked chart, no install button. Nothing here is bought, so nothing here is merchandised.

Not a list of links. Every entry carries four facts a link cannot: what it does, who made it, how many neighbors used it, and what it touches. The touch strip is the load-bearing one, and it is on the card, not one tap away.

Not sorted by winner. The featured slot is the most used this month, so it rotates. A permanent leaderboard tells a new builder the slots are taken.

The metric

Downloads measure a decision made before the thing was used. Stars measure who felt strongly. Neighbors who used it this month is the only number that means the app is still alive, and it decays honestly when a creation goes stale.

The touch strip is on the card, not behind a tap. If what an app can reach is only visible on the screen after the one where a resident decided, then the decision was made without it. Two chips is the target, three the ceiling, and the ones that matter get the terracotta inset. A creation that touches nothing consequential shows the reassuring absence instead: nothing leaves town is a chip, because a blank space is not an answer. On the dense row the strip collapses to a single dot with a title, and the count is the only number, since a row that tries to say everything stops being a row.

  1. 1
    Host chrome. Ours.

    Rendered by the shell, outside the frame. The name, the maker and the back button are ours to write, and a creation cannot reach a single pixel of this strip.

  2. 2
    The badge. The load-bearing pixel.

    The one piece of chrome a creation can never draw over. That is what makes it structurally unable to imitate Town Square: a resident always has a frame of reference the guest cannot touch, so a fake sign-in drawn inside the frame still sits under a badge that says the thing below it is somebody's bundle. There is no login form anywhere inside a creation for one to imitate, and there never will be.

  3. 3
    The seam. A different registrable domain.

    Not a policy, the cookie jar. The session cookie is structurally unable to reach the guest and the browser puts it in another process. The only channel across is one MessagePort, and the bridge checks every call against the frozen manifest on the host side, so a hand-written message that skips the SDK still gets permission_denied.

  4. 4
    The creation. Theirs.

    Luis's HTML, Luis's CSS, Luis's judgment about what a burrito score means. It looks native because the host injects the town's design tokens as CSS custom properties, so var(--ts-terracotta) resolves for him too and costs him nothing to adopt. A town that reskins Town Square reskins every creation with it.

  5. 5
    Footer chrome. Ours, and deliberately below.

    Report sits outside the frame so a resident reporting a creation is always talking to Town Square and never to the thing they are reporting. Putting it inside would be the single most obvious hole in the design.

Ownership is carried by a label and an edge treatment, never by color alone: ours has a solid navy rule and the word Town Square, theirs has a dashed terracotta outline and the word Guest bundle. The dashes are doing real work here, because the seam is the one boundary in the product where being unsure which side you are on is a security failure rather than a cosmetic one.

Host chrome, four states the strip grows downward; the badge never moves, because a badge that moves can be predicted and covered

Trust sheet, three permission sets generated from the frozen manifest, so a creation cannot write its own trust page

Grouped by consequence, not by capability. What leaves the visit and what leaves town get the terracotta inset rule and sit at the top; background is everything that is true of every creation and reads as reassurance. Absence is stated as loudly as presence, because can't reach anything outside town is the most reassuring line on the screen and it only means something because it is generated from the same field that would otherwise list a host. Three manifests are shown, so the design is proven against the boring case and the alarming one rather than the demo one.

You do not have to open this. Nothing on this page is an accusation. The committee approved it because it declared everything honestly, which is a different question from whether you want it.

Reviewed 2 August 2026, version 0.3.1. Nine residents have opened it.

The alarming manifest gets no red, no warning triangle and no scare copy. It gets a count, a truthful qualifier (two of them are not maps), the primary action demoted to sit beside Not now, and one sentence saying it is fine to walk away. Making this screen frightening would teach residents to fear the trust sheet rather than read it, and the sheet is only useful if they read it every time. The tally line at the top is the whole design: it makes the sheet skimmable without making it skippable.

Write-back consent attribution is automatic and cannot be forged, so the sheet says so rather than asking you to trust it

This is the moment the build layer actually compounds: a creation asking to put a fact into the town under a resident's name. Three things make the sheet honest. It shows the payload, field by field, because "allow Flock Camera Map to write records" is a sentence nobody can evaluate. Attribution is stated as a property of the platform, not a promise: the builder never touches it, which is precisely why it cannot be forged. And there is no delete, so the sheet says that out loud rather than letting a resident assume an undo exists. Revert is a platform operation the committee performs; a creation cannot invoke one.

Writing to the town needs vouches Six neighbors have vouched for you, ten does it. Anything you post carries your name permanently, so the bar is people, not a form.

not_verified from the bridge. The blame lands on a state, never on the resident, and it comes with the one next step that changes the state.

Why the payload is shown raw

Field names in mono, values in prose. A resident does not need to know what lng means to see that this creation is sending four things and not forty, and a builder debugging a schema gets the same screen. One surface, two readers.

Scope of "always allow"

Per creation and per record type. A creation that later declares a second type has to ask again, which closes the obvious hole: get a broad grant while you are harmless, then widen what you write.

What is deliberately missing

No "remember for all creations". A blanket write grant across the build layer would make the consent sheet a formality within a week, and the sheet is the only thing standing between a resident's name and forty independently written apps.

The sheet is ours

Drawn by the shell over the frame, with the eyebrow saying so. The creation asked; Town Square is the one doing the asking.

Boot and failure, five states the blame goes to the code, never to the resident, and never to a "network error" they cannot act on
Booting · 320px skeleton
starting Flock Camera Map…

Layered over the mount point, never in place of it. A display: none iframe is never loaded by the browser, so the handshake never happens, so it never becomes ready, so it stays hidden and then fails with a timeout that reads like the creation's fault. Found by the boundary suite.

Integrity failure

We stopped this one before it ran

The files do not match what the committee reviewed. That can be a bad upload or something worse, and either way it is not going to run until a person has looked.

v1.2.0 · bundle digest mismatch · Marta has been told

The only failure with no Try again. Retry on a bundle that failed its own hash is an invitation to keep trying until it works, which is exactly the wrong instinct here.

Hung · never called app.ready()

This one didn't finish loading

It connected but never finished rendering. Its builder has been told, and nothing you did caused it.

v0.4.2 · ready timeout after 10s

Ten seconds under height: auto, then this rather than an empty box. An empty box is the state that makes a resident blame their phone.

A denied host does not kill the creation. The CSP blocked an undeclared request, the chrome says which one in our voice, and the rest of Wade's app keeps working. Exfiltration risk is visible in the manifest rather than buried in code, and this row is that promise being kept out loud.

The source
6 files, 41 KB. No build step, everything vendored.
  • townsquare.json
  • index.html
  • app.js
  • styles.css
  • icon.svg
  • vendor/leaflet.js

Town Square keeps the source, not just the bundle. That is what the committee reads, and it is what makes the next line possible.

Forking gives you your own copy, your own slug, and an empty storage. Marta keeps hers. You would be the ninth person to fork something in Russellville.

No rating, anywhere

A five-star average on a thing your neighbor made for free is a small cruelty and a bad signal. The page carries usage, contributor count and version history instead, all of which are facts rather than opinions.

Version history is a permissions history

Each entry says whether the ask grew, and who reviewed it. Publish something harmless, build an audience, then push an update that asks for more is the browser-extension attack, and it works precisely where updates are rubber-stamped. Permission expansion always forces a human, and the history makes that visible after the fact too.

The defines block, in public

Showing the schema and the two creations already reading it is how compounding becomes legible. A resident sees their contribution feeding somebody else's app, and a builder sees a type they can use instead of inventing a parallel one.

Fork is the last thing on the page

Not because it is least important, but because it lands after a resident has read what this one does and decided they want a version of it. It is the invitation with a running start.

Builder profile a neighbor with a page, not a developer account; no follower count, no streak, no contribution graph

Marta's page shows what she built and who vouched for her. It does not show where she lives, because Town Square never stored that.

Vouches are the only status

Fourteen neighbors, three of them shown by face. There is no reputation score, no badge tier and no leaderboard, because the moment building earns status people build for status.

The retired app stays

Dimmed, with the reason. The city put out its own is a good outcome and hiding it would make the page a highlight reel. A builder who can retire something gracefully is a builder who ships a second thing.

Verified never means identified

The page is a real name because Marta chose to use one. Pseudonymity holds either way, the identity surface a creation sees is still only { handle, verified }, and no address exists to leak.

Gallery at n=3 – launch week
Russellville · the build layer

Three so far

The build layer opened eleven days ago. There are three creations, all made by people who live here, and each one exists because somebody wanted an answer.

  1. 01
    Flock Camera Map

    Marta wanted to know how many license plate readers were up on Arkansas Avenue. She asked the city, did not get a number, and built the map instead. 41 of them now.

    MK Marta Keener, library desk
  2. 02
    Burrito Index

    Luis was tired of the same argument every Friday, so he made everybody put a number on it. Fourteen kitchens, 391 plates rated.

    LR Luis Ramírez, welds at the plant
  3. 03
    Lake Level

    Wade fishes Illinois Bayou and got sick of three tabs, so now the pool stage sits next to the ten-year average on one screen.

    WC Wade Colvin, retired from the co-op
What people are asking for
  • Which pool is open this week Asked by 23 residents
  • A map of where the food trucks park Asked by 17 residents
  • School closings that beat the TV station Asked by 14 residents

Nothing here is going to be filled by a company. Three of you have already done it.

A gallery at n=3 is a real design problem and the fix is not a grid. Three cards in a three-column layout reads as a failed store. Three numbered entries with a sentence each about why the person built it reads as the beginning of something, and it is the same three rows of data. The second half of the screen is the honest inversion: a list of what residents have asked for that nobody has built, with a button that hands the request to whoever is reading. At n=3 the most valuable thing the gallery can show is the gap, and the gap is only embarrassing if you pretend it is not there. At n=40 that list becomes the smallest section on the page.

Pinning a pinned creation earns a line on Today, which is the only real reward the platform hands out
The control · three states

A toggle, not a subscribe. Pinning changes one resident's own home screen and notifies nobody, which is why it needs no confirmation and no undo toast. The disabled state names what is missing rather than just going grey.

Four is the cap. Today is a screen about the town, and a fifth pin turns the top of it into a launcher. A resident at the ceiling is offered a swap, never a longer list.

A pinned line shows the last thing the creation reported through app.setTitle, with the time it said it. Town Square does not run three apps in the background to keep those numbers fresh, so it says how old they are instead of pretending.

The stale timestamp is the whole specimen. Every instinct says run the creations on a schedule so Today is live. That means executing three residents' bundles on a cadence nobody consented to, on battery, for a number. The honest version costs one line of type: show the last reported title and say when it was said. A resident learns instantly which pins are worth a tap, and the platform never quietly becomes a background job runner for arbitrary code.

The invitation, three intensities no counter, no urgency, no reward; the pitch is that it takes a weekend and a neighbor reads it
1. Footer line · everywhere, permanent

Every one of these was made by somebody who lives here.

One sentence of fact and one link. It sits under the gallery, under a creation's footer chrome, and under a builder profile. Present enough to be noticed on the fourth visit, quiet enough to never be in the way on the first.

2. Gallery card · once, at the bottom of the list
Build one

Describe what you want to the AI tool you already use, connect it to Town Square, and a neighbor on the review committee reads it before it goes up. Most of these took a weekend.

The dashed edge is doing a job: it is the one card in the gallery that is not a creation, and it should read as an empty slot waiting for somebody rather than as an advertisement.

3. Interstitial – asked for, never sprung
The build layer

You do not need permission, and you do not need to be a programmer.

Twelve people in Russellville have built something on Town Square. Two of them had written code before.

  1. 1
    Tell your AI tool what you want Claude, ChatGPT, whatever you already use. "A map of the free little libraries in town, where anybody can add one."
  2. 2
    Point it at Town Square One connection, one time. Your tool then knows the whole contract: what it can read, what it can write, and how to ask.
  3. 3
    Send it over A neighbor on the committee reads what it asks for and what it does. Usually a few days. They will tell you what to fix rather than just saying no.
  4. 4
    It is in the town Running sandboxed, in the town's own type and color, with your name on it. Anything it records becomes something the next person can build on.

I thought you had to be a programmer. I described it out loud, the same way I would explain it to somebody at the desk, and it mostly wrote itself. The part I did was knowing what the town needed.

MK Marta Keener, Flock Camera Map

Free, and it stays yours. Nobody is paid for anything in the gallery, and Town Square takes no cut of anything, because there is nothing to take a cut of.

What makes this not a growth prompt

It never interrupts. The interstitial is reached by tapping How it works, never shown on a timer, a visit count, or after a resident finishes something. A modal nobody asked for is the exact move this section is defined against.

No counter, no scarcity, no reward. No "join 340 builders", no launch deadline, no badge at the end. The offer is that a small thing you want to exist can exist, and the honest cost is a weekend and a neighbor reading your code.

It names the hard part correctly. Step one is describing the thing, and the pull quote says the work was knowing what the town needed. Telling a library clerk that the coding is easy is only credible if you also tell her which part is not.

It admits the wait. Review takes a few days and the page says so. A build funnel that hides its slowest step gets one enthusiastic resident and then never sees them again.

The one dark screen

The interstitial inverts because it is the only full-screen interruption in the whole section, and because the featured card has already trained the eye that dark means this is the build layer. Two dark surfaces in the section, both about the same idea.

07

The builder door

Connect an AI tool you already pay for, build against the SDK, validate, preview on a real sandbox, submit for review. Town Square generates nothing and pays for nothing. Every screen here sits behind one link, because a resident who never builds should never meet any of it.

Front door, hero says what it costs you before it says what you get
Build on Town Square

Russellville runs on things somebody made.

If you can describe an app, your AI tool can build it, and this town square can host it. A trail conditions board. A map of every Flock camera anyone has spotted. A list of who still has generators after an ice storm.

Connect your AI tool Read the SDK first

14 creations live. Last one published Tuesday by @oldpost.

Front door, the three steps three, and the third one is a person reading your code
1

Connect

Mint a token here, paste one line into Claude Code. Your tool now knows the SDK, the manifest format, and Russellville's real data.

about two minutes

2

Build and preview

Describe what you want. Your tool writes it, checks it against our rules, and puts it on a live sandbox address you can open on your phone.

an evening, usually

3

Submit for review

Someone on the review committee reads your source and your permissions, then approves it or tells you what to change. Updates get read too.

usually under three days

Front door, the honest prerequisite the one card that is allowed to talk someone out of it

You will need an AI tool of your own

Town Square does not write apps for you. There is no chat box here. You bring a tool you already have, it does the writing, and the cost of that writing is yours, not the town's. That is why this is free to host.

  • Claude Code, in a terminal. What we build against, and the smoothest path.
  • Claude Desktop or anything else that speaks MCP. Works, with a little more setup.
  • A phone alone is not enough yet. You need a computer you can run a command on.

You do not need to know JavaScript. You do need to be willing to read what your tool wrote, because you are the one submitting it and your name goes on it.

The temptation on this page is to write anyone in town can make an app, because it is the sentence the thesis wants to be true. It is not true today. What is true is anyone with an AI subscription and a laptop, and a builder who discovers the gap after signing up is a builder who does not come back. So the hero promises a specific, local, buildable thing, the prerequisite card is allowed to say no, and the tone stays flat and unhurried rather than encouraging. Warmth is earned later, at the first publish, where it costs nobody anything.

This whole section lives behind one link in the site footer and one card in Settings. Nothing in the resident tab bar points here, no banner suggests it, and a resident who reads the paper and checks the weekend never sees a token, a manifest, or the word MCP. The build layer is where the value compounds, but it is not where most people live, and cluttering the reading path to advertise it would trade the many for the few.

Connect, step one: name the token a label is the only field, because the scopes are not yours to choose

New connection

What this token can do
  • Read the SDK and templates. Docs, examples, starting shapes.
  • Read Russellville's public data. Events, notices, businesses, shared records. The same things any resident can see.
  • Create and preview drafts you own. Nobody else's drafts, ever.
  • Submit for review. Submit, not publish. There is no token that skips the committee.

These are fixed. A token that could do less would not be useful, and a token that could do more does not exist.

Code block, a file filename header, line numbers, copy; light because you read it like a document

No author and no id. The platform assigns both from whoever submitted, because a manifest that names its own author is an impersonation hole and one that names its own id is slug squatting.

Code block, an SDK call same component, line numbers off, because eight lines do not need addressing
Terminal transcript dark, no filename, a prompt glyph; it is a recording of a session, not a file you edit
~/creations/flock-camera-map 
$ claude> map the Flock cameras people have reported around towntownsquare whoami            @wgatlin, verified residenttownsquare get_sdk_docs      sdk 1, 14 methods, hash 9f2c…townsquare list_record_types flock_camera already exists, defined by @oldposttownsquare scaffold          template: map-over-recordstownsquare begin_upload      12 files, 148 KB declared$ curl -s --upload-file ... # 12 of 12 uploadedtownsquare validate          8 passed, 1 warning, 0 errorstownsquare preview           https://p-3f9c2a.townsquare-apps.netOpen that in a browser. Your app's console errors show upthere, not here.$

The bytes never travel through the model. The agent declares a path, a sha256 and a length for every file, gets a one-time ticket, and one shell command moves the actual bytes. A file in the upload that was not in the inventory is rejected, which is what turns "everything is vendored" from a promise into a check.

Two code treatments, on purpose. A file is light, titled, numbered and copyable, because you read it, quote a line of it to someone, and paste it into an editor. A terminal is dark with a prompt glyph and no line numbers, because line 7 of a transcript is not a thing anyone refers to. Syntax colour is the same four registers everywhere: navy for the words the language owns, terracotta for anything quoted, sage for bare values, muted ink for comments. Four is enough to read structure and few enough that a code block never out-shouts the page it sits on.

Permission row the machine value and its consequence sit on one line, so declaring is never abstract

What this creation may reach

A reviewer decides from this block alone, usually in under a minute. Everything not declared here is refused at runtime even if your code tries.

"identity": "handle"

Your app can ask who is signed in and gets back a handle and whether they are verified. Never an email, never a real name, never a location.

"read": ["flock_camera"]

Your app can list every camera anyone in town has recorded, including ones added by other creations. @oldpost defined this type in March and 340 rows already exist.

"write": ["flock_camera"]

Your app can add and edit cameras, and every change is stamped with the resident who made it and with your creation. This is the one a reviewer will ask you about, so say in your note why it needs it.

"storage": false

Off. Turn it on only if you save something per person, like a filter they picked. 64 KB each, private to them, invisible to every other creation.

"device": []

Not available yet. Geolocation and camera access land in a later SDK. The field exists now so a map has somewhere to ask later without breaking every manifest written before it.

Network allowlist entry a hostname, and underneath it the exact policy line a human will approve
tile.openstreetmap.org map tiles
What the reviewer will see, and what the browser will enforce
img-src     'self' data: tile.openstreetmap.orgconnect-src 'self' tile.openstreetmap.orgscript-src  'self'  // never yours to change

Declared hosts reach four directives and no more: connect-src, img-src, media-src, font-src. script-src stays 'self' no matter what you write here, which is the mechanism that makes vendoring real rather than a rule nobody checks.

Images are in that list on purpose. Lock down fetch and leave images open and new Image().src = 'https://…?' + secret still walks data out the door without ever needing a reply.

Defining a record type the one place a builder is creating something the whole town inherits

This creation defines a new kind of record

town-wide, forever
FieldTypeRequiredLimitsRemove
trail string required one of: Bona Dea, Old Post Road, Lake Dardanelle, Prairie Creek
status string required one of: clear, muddy, flooded, closed
note string optional maxLength 500
checked_on date required no limit

Read this before you save. Once trail_condition exists, any other creation in Russellville can ask to read it, and nobody, including you, can ever retype or remove a field. Later creations may add optional fields. That is the entire list of changes that will ever be allowed.

You do not own this type. If you stop maintaining this app, the data stays and someone else picks it up. That is the point of it.

No conflict. Russellville has 6 record types and none is named trail_condition.

The permissions block is the reviewer's entire job, so the authoring surface has to slow a builder down at exactly the moment their AI tool has offered to move fast. Three choices do that. The consequence sits beside the value, in the second person, so nobody declares write without reading what write means. The compiled CSP is shown while you type, because the thing being approved is a policy string and hiding it until review means the builder is surprised twice. And defines carries a plainly worded permanence warning, because additive-only forever is genuinely unusual and a builder who learns it from a rejection learned it too late.

Validation results, mixed one blocker, one warning, the rest folded away; errors carry a file, a line and the fix

One thing is blocking

Fix it and this is ready to submit. The queue runs this exact same check, so a clean result here means the queue accepts it.

1 error 1 warning 8 passed
dynamic_record_type app.js:88

records.list(kind) is called with a variable. A reviewer reading this file cannot tell what your app reads, so neither can we.

Pass the type as a plain string: records.list('flock_camera'). If you need two types, write two calls and declare both.

over_declared_permission townsquare.json:19

"storage": true is declared but storage.get and storage.set are never called anywhere in the bundle.

Set it to false. This will not block you, but a permissions block full of things you do not use is a slower review, and AI tools ask for storage out of habit.

vendoring 12 files

Every import resolves inside your bundle. vendor/maplibre.js is a real file, not a CDN link, so this app still works in five years when that CDN does not.

network_hosts townsquare.json:20

One outbound host found in the code, tile.openstreetmap.org, and it is the one you declared. Nothing else in this bundle talks to the outside.

Errors are terracotta, not brick. Brick is the flood siren, and spending it on a missing comma means it says nothing at 6am when the river is actually up.

Preview real hosting on a real other domain, said plainly rather than framed as a mockup
p-3f9c2a.townsquare-apps.net
340 cameras mapped last added on E Main at Arkansas Ave

This is not a mockup. It is your bundle, on a real address, under the same sandbox, the same bridge and the same compiled policy a published creation runs under. Anything that works here works after approval, and anything blocked here would have been blocked there.

The address is on townsquare-apps.net, a different domain from Russellville's own on purpose, so the browser puts your app in its own process and your Town Square session cookie is structurally unable to reach it. Link expires in 24 hours and only you can open it.

Review status, the whole ladder shape and word carry the state, colour only reinforces it
Draft Submitted In review Changes requested Approved Live Live, v1.1.0 v1.2.0 in review

The last one is the state that matters most and the easiest to forget to design. An approved creation keeps serving its approved version while its update waits. Nobody gets the unreviewed one, which is exactly how a well-behaved app becomes a malicious one everywhere else this has been tried.

A submission, in full the reviewer's note is a person writing to a neighbour, not a rejection code

A rejection with no reason is how a light-touch community turns into a bureaucracy people route around. So the note is free prose from a named neighbour, not a checkbox, and it is allowed to open by saying the app is good. Two structural choices back that up: the mechanical checks run first so a reviewer never spends goodwill on a missing comma, and the permissions diff is what the reviewer is actually reading, which is why Dana's note is about a capability that was not there in v1.1.0 rather than about code style.

A phone cannot run Claude Code, so the phone build of this path deliberately does nothing. It reads status, it shows the reviewer's note in full, and it says out loud that the next step is on a computer.
