SDK reference five namespaces, and every method states the permission it needs before the example
town
info() thisWeek() items() businesses()
user
current()
records
list() get() create() update() history()
storage
get() set()
app
ready() setHeight() setTitle()
await records.create(type, data) needs write

Adds one record of a type your manifest declares under permissions.write. Attribution is automatic: the acting resident and your creation are both stamped on the row, and you cannot set either, which is precisely why neither can be forged.

Parameters
type string literal
The record type, written out as a quoted string. A variable here is a validation error, because a reviewer cannot see what an app writes if the source does not say it.
data object
Must match the type's schema. Anything extra is rejected rather than ignored.
Returns
{ id: 'rec_8fJ2q', version: 1, created_at: '2026-08-05T14:02:11Z' }
Example
Throws
  • not_verifiedSigned in, but neighbours have not vouched yet. Not retryable.
  • unauthenticatedSigned out. The common case, so handle it first.
  • permission_deniedThe type is not in your manifest's write list.
  • invalid_recordPayload does not match the schema.
  • rate_limitedCarries retry_after. One of only two worth retrying.
Machine-readable docs callout an LLM writes most of these, so the docs have a second audience that does not click

Your AI tool should read this, not you

Everything on this page is generated from the SDK source, so it cannot drift from what actually runs. The same artifact is served three ways, and the MCP server refuses to start if the three disagree.

  • llms.txtthe whole contract as one flat file, for pasting into any tool
  • AGENTS.mdships inside every scaffold, so a coding agent picks up the rules without being told
  • get_sdk_docsthe MCP tool, which is what your tool will actually call first

Version sdk 1, hash 9f2c41a8. SDK 1 never breaks. Things get added, nothing gets removed, because no resident is going to come back and maintain an app they made one Saturday.

08

Identity, vouching, and moderation

Signing in, being vouched for by a neighbour, and the light-touch committee that keeps the place honest. Town Square never stores an address, and being verified never means being publicly identified. A vouch is a warm gesture between two people who know each other, so it has to look like one and not like a background check.

The whole design problem of this section is that verification is social, and social gates go wrong in one of two directions. Too heavy and it reads as a background check, which loses exactly the privacy-minded residents most likely to build something. Too eager and it becomes a growth loop that pressures people into asking strangers for favours. Everything below is tuned between those: the ladder never shames a resident at zero, the ask surface has no reminders and no counters, and the only place a chain is ever shown is an admin screen.

Sign in, magic link One form, one answer. The copy must never become the oracle the API refused to be.

Choosing a handle Availability resolves in the field, never on submit. A rejected form after the fact reads as a refusal.
What a handle is for

A handle is what the town sees. It is the only name Town Square has for you, and your real one is never asked for, never stored and never inferred.

  • Use your name if you want to. Plenty of people do.
  • Use anything else if you would rather. Being verified does not require being identified.
  • Changeable once every 30 days. Old handles are retired, never reissued.
A neighbour vouching for you knows who you are already. That is the point. The rest of the town does not need to.

An admin can raise this for a long-standing resident, or lower it to zero for a new account. Ten is only the default.

What a creation is handed

A resident-built creation runs in a sandboxed frame and asks the shell who is signed in. This is the entire answer, for everyone, forever.

{
  "handle": "westside_ruth",
  "verified": true
}

No email. No id it can join on. No method, no date, no vouch count, no anything a creation could use to build a second identity graph on top of ours. If a creation needs more than a name and a yes, the answer is that it does not.

The shell owns this shape. A creation cannot widen it, and the review reads the manifest to be sure it never asked to.

Why this surfaced
  • Eleven vouches in forty minutes, against a rolling budget of ten. One was an override raised in June.
  • Every account created inside the same hour, none of them vouched for by anybody else.
  • No handle in the group has read, saved, or opened anything since.

This is a heuristic, not a verdict. It ranks a branch for a human to read. Nothing is acted on automatically, ever.

Revoked. Here is what did and did not happen.
  • Eleven vouches marked revoked, by @cravenshall, 5 August.
  • The branch under each is flagged for review and queued under Flagged contributions.
  • Each account is told once, in plain words, that a moderator is reading.
  • Nobody was un-verified automatically. Revoking never cascades.
  • Nothing was deleted. Not an account, not a creation, not a record version.

Cascading would be one click and would also destroy the legitimate vouches a bad actor happened to give. In a town this size that is a real cost paid by real neighbours, so the blunt version is not on the screen.

Reporting, from the chrome and never from the thing being reported Quiet by design. No counts, no public marks, no promise of an outcome, so it cannot be used as a vote.

Report Bona Dea trail conditions

Town Square follows the law and does not referee taste. What gets acted on is mostly the first two.

One category, one box. More fields would make a report feel like paperwork and would collect things a moderator does not need.

Report Bona Dea trail conditions

Sent. A moderator will read it. Most reports are read and closed with nothing else happening, and that is normal.

Already reported

You had already reported this, so we kept your first report rather than adding another.

Not a thank you, and not a second report. Pretending a duplicate counted would turn the queue into a tally and reporting into a campaign.

Report Bona Dea trail conditions

Reporting is for verified residents, so a moderator knows a neighbour is behind it. Someone who is already verified can vouch for you from their account page.

Said before the form, not after the send. Filling in a box that was never going to go anywhere is worse than never seeing the box.

What reporting is not
  • It does not say how many others reported the same thing.
  • It never marks the creation publicly while it is open.
  • It does not tell the builder who reported them.
  • It promises no outcome and gives no status thread.

Every one of those exists on the platforms this is explicitly not. A visible count is a pile-on button, a public mark is a scarlet letter, and a status thread turns a neighbour's quiet note into a case they now have to follow.

The one thing a reporter gets is an email when the report is closed, saying what was concluded. Often that is "we read it, nothing needed to happen".

Who decides things here

Three neighbours, named, with a five line policy

Moderation is a role, not a person. Anyone on this list can be scoped in or out by an admin, and the list changes in public.

  • CH
    @cravenshall admin
    Since March. Runs the Bona Dea trail cleanup. Holds the revert button and the vouch chain viewer.
  • MA
    @mainstreetmarcy moderator
    Since May. Downtown, keeps most of the business hours current. Reads reports and decides submissions.
  • AM
    @techdrive_amir moderator
    Since July. Reads code, so most creation reviews land with him. Recuses himself on his own submissions.
The whole policy
  1. Town Square follows the law. That is the floor and most of the ceiling.
  2. Code that runs in a neighbour's browser is read before it runs. Every version, including updates.
  3. Nothing is deleted. Things get hidden, reverted, or put back.
  4. Every action is logged with who did it and why, and the log is readable by any verified resident.
  5. We do not referee taste, tone, or who is right about the school board.

Five lines, because a policy nobody finishes reading is a policy nobody can hold you to. Last changed 14 June, and the change is in the log.

Account settings, and the honest version of what we hold Written for a resident to read once and stop wondering. The delete consequences are stated in full, including what cannot be undone.

Account and privacy

Five switches and no marketing category, because there is nothing to market. Off by default for the two that are not about something you did.

Account – what we hold
In plain English

What we hold about you

  • Your handle, @westside_ruth, which the town sees.
  • Your email, which nobody sees. It signs you in and lets a moderator reach you.
  • The date you joined.
  • Three facts about verification: that you are verified, that the method was vouch, and that it happened on 14 July.
  • Which handles vouched for you and which you vouched for. Committee only.
  • What you built and what you changed, with the date.
And what we do not
  • Your address. Not hashed, not once, not ever. There is no column.
  • Your real name, unless you typed it into your handle yourself.
  • Your phone number.
  • Where you are, or where you were. No location, no IP log past the day.
  • What you read. Browsing is not tied to your account.
The postcard method, if a town ever turns it on, touches an address once to mail it and never hands it to us. That is the design, not the promise.
Account – export and delete
Your copy
Download everything we hold
One JSON file, ready in about a minute. It is short.
Leaving
Delete my account

Straight answers, so nothing here surprises you afterwards.

  • Your email is deleted. Sign-in stops working immediately.
  • Your verification record is deleted.
  • The vouches you gave are withdrawn. Those branches get flagged for a moderator to read, and nobody is un-verified by it.
  • Your handle is retired, not freed. Nobody can take @westside_ruth afterwards.
  • Versions you wrote stay, still attributed to the retired handle. Town history cannot be rewritten by one person leaving, and that is the point of it.
  • Creations you published keep running unless you take them down first.

The destructive button is the plainer of the two, and the softer path is listed first. Neither is red, because red here would be theatre and the alarm colour belongs to the river.

What this section refuses to build, on purpose. A public vouch count on a profile, which would make verification a status. A "verified since" badge on every post, which turns pseudonymity into a two-tier town. A report count, which is a pile-on button. Auto-cascade on a revoked vouch, which is one click of admin convenience paid for by ten innocent neighbours. And a growth loop on the ask surface, which is the exact move that turns a community platform into the thing everyone left. Every one of those was cheap to add and each is a step toward the app this is explicitly not.

09

Civic, notices, and emergency

City hall, the notice ladder, and the one screen that is allowed to take over the phone. The emergency register exists so that every ordinary day can stay calm, which means most of this section is about restraint: four severities and no more, one alarm colour used once per screen, and a default subscription that will not wake anyone up for a planning commission agenda.

The severity ladder, all four together ships as .notice; the only tinted card on the screen, and most days it is not rendered at all
Informationalin app only
Advisoryquiet push
Urgentpush, bar, takeover
Emergencybreaks through silent
Informational Leaf and limb pickup starts Monday on the east side Piles at the curb by 6 am. Sanitation is running the Weir Road and Skyline routes first. City of Russellville, Sanitation · fetched 6:10 am Advisory Arkansas River is forecast to reach 22.4 ft at Dardanelle by Thursday Action stage is 23 ft. Low-lying access at Old Post Road park may close if it keeps rising. NWS Little Rock, river forecast · fetched 5:45 am Urgent Boil order for everything north of Main between Denver and Knoxville Bring water to a rolling boil for one minute before drinking or cooking. In effect until two clear samples come back, expected Friday. Russellville Water Utility · fetched 11 minutes ago Emergency Tornado warning for Russellville and central Pope County until 11:45 pm Take shelter now. Interior room, lowest floor, away from windows. NWS Little Rock · issued 11:04 pm

Four, not seven. Every severity level you add is a level someone has to learn, and the ones in the middle are the ones nobody can tell apart. A resident does not need to know the difference between a level 3 and a level 4; they need to know four things, in this order: is this for me, is it happening now, do I have to do something, and does it wake me up. Four levels answer that with one question each. Informational is news you would want anyway. Advisory is a condition to be aware of. Urgent changes what you do today. Emergency changes what you do in the next ten minutes. Seven levels would only give the middle three a false precision no source actually supplies – the National Weather Service publishes watch, advisory, and warning; the water utility publishes an order or nothing. We are mapping upstream vocabularies, not inventing one, and the ladder has to be lossy in the safe direction. When a source is ambiguous we round down, then let the resident raise their own threshold. Colour is never the carrier: each notice states its severity in words above the headline, because the whole ladder has to survive a screenshot, a screen reader, and colour blindness.

The dismissal is the hard part. An X in the top corner trains people to close the screen before they read it, and it puts the escape at the exact spot a thumb lands when a phone buzzes at 11pm. So there is no X. The dismissal sits at the bottom, after the instruction and after the source, it is a full sentence, and it says what it does: hide this until it changes. Any update from the source brings it straight back, and hiding never unsubscribes. The one action is one action, always: a second button here is a decision, and a decision at 11pm is a delay. Everything else on the screen is text you can act on without tapping anything, because the most likely outcome is that the phone gets put down and the person moves. After it clears, the takeover does not just vanish – it becomes a calm card with the whole sequence in it, because the question the next morning is always "what actually happened last night", and if we do not answer it the answer comes from a rumour.

The mark on the takeover the open problem, and the fix that needs no new asset
Shipping today full-colour mark
Relayed by Town Square

Terracotta bubble, navy figures, cream tile. Three extra colours land two inches under a brick alarm band and the screen stops being one register.

Tempting mono knockout
Relayed by Town Square

Needs a purpose-built mono lockup that does not exist, and the real mark's internal separations are thin strokes that vanish flattened at 22px. It also still spends a look on our logo.

Proposed no mark, source first
National Weather Service, Little Rock
Issued 11:04 pm · relayed by Town Square

Attribution becomes typographic. The brand survives as five words in the quietest line on the screen, and the mark comes back on the what-happened card where the register is neutral again.

The resolution is removal, not redrawing. The mark's job is to tell you which app you are in, and on a takeover that is the one thing the person already knows – their own phone woke them up. Worse, the mark at the attribution point implies we are the source. We are not. The National Weather Service issued the warning; we carried it. Putting our logo where the issuing agency's name belongs is a small credit-taking that becomes a real problem the first time an alert is wrong. So the takeover carries no mark at all, the source agency gets the emphatic line, and "relayed by Town Square" is a clause in the quiet line underneath. This ships today with no asset work, which is the argument that settles it: the mono lockup is still worth commissioning for dark headers elsewhere, but it was never the fix for this screen.

The alert bar, collapsed and expanded a takeover is for the first ten minutes; day three of a river rise needs a bar you can live above
Collapsed – the persistent form, 44px, above the header on every screen
Advisory River at 22.9 ft and rising, action stage is 23
Town SquareRussellville
Expanded – tap once, it pushes the page down rather than covering it
Advisory River at 22.9 ft and rising, action stage is 23

Dardanelle gauge read 22.9 ft at 5 am, up 0.4 ft overnight. NWS expects a crest near 23.6 ft Friday afternoon. At 23 ft the low road into Old Post Road park floods and the boat ramp closes.

Gauge and forecast What floods at each stage

Urgent, still a bar – the takeover already happened, this is what is left

The bar is the answer to the thing that actually kills emergency design: a situation that lasts four days. A takeover on day one is right and a takeover on day three is an app you delete. So urgency decays on a schedule the resident can feel – a takeover collapses to a bar after the first view or after 30 minutes, whichever comes first, and the bar collapses to a line. It never covers content, it pushes content, because anything that covers the page in a long situation gets swiped away reflexively and takes the real update with it. The one control that is not an action is "keep collapsed until the number changes": people will absolutely mute a four-day river, and the honest move is to give them a mute that re-arms itself rather than let them turn the whole thing off.

Item detail, the plain-terms panel we describe the document, we never grade it; every claim points at a page
Ordinance 2568 Second reading On the agenda for tonight, item 3

An ordinance rezoning 4.1 acres at the corner of East Main Street and North Arkansas Avenue from R-1 single family to C-2 general commercial

In plain terms
  • The land is the old Dawson nursery lot, vacant since 2019. p. 2
  • R-1 allows single family houses. C-2 allows retail, restaurants, offices, and a drive-through with a conditional use permit. p. 3, Table 4
  • The applicant is Arkansas Valley Holdings LLC. The ordinance does not name a tenant or a building. p. 1
  • A rezoning does not approve a specific project. Anything built would come back for site plan review. p. 4
  • Planning Commission recommended approval 5 to 1 on 8 May. Their recommendation is advisory. minutes, p. 3
  • Second reading means the council may vote tonight, or suspend the rules and pass it on third reading the same night. p. 4

Every line above restates something the document says and links the page it says it on. We do not say whether a rezoning is good for the neighbourhood, we do not count the letters for and against, and we do not describe anyone's motive. Where the packet is silent, we write that it is silent rather than filling it in.

In the packet
Ordinance text, 4 pp Site map and legal description Correspondence, 14 letters, 22 pp Planning Commission minutes, 8 May
How it got here
  1. 17 MarApplication filed
  2. 08 MayPlanning Commission, recommended 5 to 1
  3. 19 MayFirst reading, no vote
  4. 02 JunSecond reading, tonight
City of Russellville, agenda packet pp. 1 to 8 · fetched 30 May 6:10 am · plain-terms lines written by a Town Square editor and checked against the pages cited

"What this actually means" is the most valuable thing on the screen and the fastest way to lose the town's trust. So the panel has a rule it cannot break: every line restates something in the document and names the page. No line may contain a judgement, a consequence we predict, a count of who is for and against, or a characterisation of anyone's motive. When the packet is silent, the panel says it is silent – "the ordinance does not name a tenant" is the single most useful line in that list, and it is pure description. The disclosure is not buried: it names a human editor, because "the AI summarised it" is not an answer anyone in a council chamber will accept.

The vote record no red and green; the outcome is a sentence and every name is on the same row treatment

The mayor was present and declined to break the tie, which the minutes record. "Failed" is stated as a word before any number, because a tally alone does not tell you which way it went.

No vote taken
Tabledno roll call

Moved to the 16 June agenda by voice vote. There is no roll to show, so we show none rather than inventing an eight-row table of dashes.

Vote records are ugly because they are built as spreadsheets, and a spreadsheet answers "what were the numbers" when the resident is asking "did it pass, and how did my ward vote." So the outcome is a word first and a tally second, the ward is printed beside every name because that is how a resident finds themselves in the list, and the roll is grouped by how people voted rather than sorted by seat. There is deliberately no red and no green: it is the one thing every civic data product reaches for and it does three bad things at once – it fails for colour blind readers, it makes a routine procedural vote look like a fight, and in this system red is spoken for. Sage marks the affirmative, a hollow ring marks the negative, and both are labelled in words, so the record survives being screenshotted into a group chat.

Alert subscriptions the threshold is a slider through the same four rungs, so the setting and the ladder are literally the same object
Settings – alerts
Alerts

What should wake you up

You are set to the default. Most people never change this, which is why the default has to be right.

Send me a push notification for
Quiet hours
10:00 pm to 6:30 am

Advisories and anything below hold until morning. An emergency always comes through, and it comes through on silent. There is no setting that turns that off, and we would rather tell you that plainly than hide it in a toggle you find at 3 am.

Also tell me about
City Council agendas
School board and closings
Planning and rezonings
Trash and recycling changes
Road closures
Arkansas Nuclear One notices

We never ask for your address. Alerts are matched to the town and to zones you pick by name, never to a location we track.

Threshold rungs, out of the phone
Everything~9 a week
Advisory and up~2 a week
Urgent and up~1 a monthDefault
Emergency onlya few a year
Switch states
Off On Focus Locked on

"Locked on" is the emergency channel. It renders as a switch so its state is legible, and it is disabled with an explanation rather than hidden, because a control you cannot find is worse than one you cannot move.

The default is urgent and up, quiet hours on, and it has to be conservative for a reason that is not politeness. Notification permission is spent once. A resident installs this in July because they want to know what is on this weekend; if the first three pushes are a planning commission agenda, a leaf pickup schedule, and a heat advisory, notifications are off by August and they are off in November when the ice storm comes. The subscription screen is therefore an argument for turning things on, made after the app has earned it, not a wall of switches at signup. Frequencies are printed next to every rung because "about 9 a week" is the only honest way to describe what a person is agreeing to, and it is the number that stops them picking Everything and regretting it. The one thing we do not let anyone turn off is the emergency channel, and we say so in a sentence instead of quietly enforcing it.

Lock screen specimens the first line has to carry the whole alert, because for most people the first line is the whole alert
Lock screen – the three that push
11:04
Wednesday, 3 June
Town Square Emergency now
Tornado warning until 11:45 pm
Take shelter now. Interior room, lowest floor, away from windows. NWS Little Rock.
Delivered on silent
Town Square Urgent 4:21 pm
Boil order north of Main
Between Denver and Knoxville. Boil one minute before drinking or cooking.
Town Square Advisory 6:02 am
River forecast to reach 23.6 ft Friday
Action stage is 23. Old Post Road park access may close.
Anatomy, at size
Town Square Emergency now
Tornado warning until 11:45 pm
Take shelter now. Interior room, lowest floor, away from windows. NWS Little Rock.
Delivered on silent
  • Severity is a word in the header, beside the app name, where iOS and Android both leave room. It is not in the title, because the title has one job.
  • The title is an instruction or a fact, never a teaser. "Tornado warning until 11:45 pm" is complete on its own. "Important weather update" is not a notification, it is an ad for one.
  • The body names the source in its last clause so a person deciding whether to believe it can, without unlocking.
  • No emoji, no siren glyph, no all caps. The escalation is carried by the words and by the fact that it arrived at all.
  • Only emergency requests the critical channel that breaks silent mode. That request is made once, at setup, and never for anything else.
Informational never pushes
There is no informational push specimen because there is no informational push. Leaf pickup, agendas, and rate schedules appear in the app and in the weekly digest. The ladder has four rungs and only three of them are allowed to reach the lock screen, which is the single most load-bearing decision in this section.

What this module will never do.
  • Rank, score, endorse, or recommend a candidate or a position.
  • Summarise what a candidate believes, or publish a photograph.
  • Reorder the list for any reason other than the alphabet.
  • Show turnout, polling, or fundraising totals during the race.
  • Accept a paid placement of any kind, in this module or beside it.
Every name links out to the county's own filing record. If a resident wants to know more, we send them to the source rather than becoming one.
Pope County Clerk, certified candidate list · Arkansas Secretary of State, election calendar · fetched 6 Oct 6:10 am

Neutrality has to be built out of layout, not promised in a policy page nobody reads. Every candidate gets the same row, the same weight, the same one link, and the alphabet decides the order – there is no editorial surface left to be biased with. No photographs, because a photograph is a persuasive object and we cannot source eight of them evenly. No summaries of a candidate's positions, because writing six of those fairly is beyond what a town platform can defend, and writing five of them fairly while getting one wrong is worse than writing none. Ballot questions are printed as certified, word for word, since a paraphrase of a ballot title is an argument about it. The list of things this module will never do is on the screen and not in a policy document, because in a town of 29,000 the person who thinks we tilted it is going to be standing in front of us at the farmers market.

Provenance the smallest line on the screen and the reason any of the rest can be believed
The footer, four freshness states
Fresh, the normal case
City of Russellville, agenda packet PDF · published 29 May 4:41 pm · fetched 11 minutes ago
Live, checked constantly
NWS Little Rock, active alerts feed · checked every 60 seconds · last 40 seconds ago
Stale – the source has gone quiet, which is not an alarm
Russellville School District, board page · nothing new since 18 April, 47 days · we are still checking every morning
Broken – we cannot reach it at all
Pope County meeting calendar · last good fetch 2 June 6:10 am · failing since yesterday, showing what we had The county's page
Stale, escalated into the card it belongs to
The school board page has not changed in 47 days

The district posts agendas on its own site and it has been quiet since 18 April. That usually means no meetings were called, but we cannot tell the difference between "nothing happened" and "nobody posted it".

Open the district's page Tell us if we are missing something

Stale is set in ink, not gold and never brick. A source going quiet is a fact about the source, and dressing it as a warning would spend the alert registers on our own plumbing. The escalated card only appears on the body's own page, never in the feed.

Attached to a real item
19May City Council, regular meeting 11 items · 4 votes taken City Clerk, approved minutes · fetched 3 Jun 6:10 am

Every civic item carries where it came from and when we got it, because the whole product is a claim about someone else's document. The line is deliberately the quietest thing in the card: it is there for the one reader in fifty who wants it, and for the argument in the comments that it settles in four words. Freshness is stated as an interval a person can feel ("11 minutes ago", "47 days") rather than a timestamp they have to do arithmetic on. And staleness is never styled as an alert. The city's website not updating is our problem to disclose, not the resident's problem to worry about – so it is grey, it says what we are still doing about it, and it links out so anyone can check us.

10

States, feedback, and motion

Town Square is assembled from a dozen scraped sources that break on their own schedule, read on one bar of signal out past Lake Dardanelle, by residents who did not sign up for anything. Every state below is a real Tuesday, not a footnote: the empties, the ladder of errors, the offline path, the stale timestamp that is the only honest signal we have, and the motion spec that ties them together.

The colour rule for this whole section. Every recoverable problem is terracotta: a field that did not validate, a save that failed, a source that stopped answering. Brick appears nowhere in this section. It is the one alarm register, and if a resident learns it means "your handle is taken" then it means nothing at 6am when the Illinois Bayou is over Weir Road. Sage is reserved for confirmed and safe, gold for civic notice, and the empties get no colour at all except one small accent mark.

Empty state anatomy four slots, three of them optional, so one component covers every empty in the product

Nothing has come in yet today.

The Courier usually posts around seven. Yesterday's front page is still here.

  1. 1 Mark. 56px, drawn, optional. Dropped in dense list slots.
  2. 2 Line. Newsreader 18px. States the fact. Never an apology.
  3. 3 Sub-line. DM Sans 15px, ink60, max 34ch. Says what happens next or what else is true.
  4. 4 Action. Optional, and only if there is genuinely somewhere better to be.

Centred when it owns the screen, left aligned when it sits in a slot. A centred empty inside a 180px card reads as a broken card. The variant is one attribute, data-align="start", and nothing else changes.

No events on the calendar for Tuesday.

Thursday has four, starting with market setup at 4.

Voice test. Read it out loud to a neighbour. "No results found" fails. "Oops, nothing here!" fails harder. "Nothing has come in yet today" is what you would actually say, and it leaves room for the possibility that something will.

Empties, resident surfaces each one written for its own surface; a shared string here would be a shared shrug

Creations, a gallery that is genuinely young

Three creations so far.

Town Square opened to builders on July 14. Everything in here was made by somebody who lives in Russellville, which is the point.

The gallery is not empty, it is young, and those are different states. Three creations render as three cards with this note underneath them, never as a void. Telling a resident "no creations yet" when there are three is a lie the product does not need to tell, and the honest version reads as momentum instead of failure.

Empties, builder and moderator one is an invitation with a next command in it, one is good news and says so
Builder, nothing published

You haven't published anything yet.

Point your AI tool at the Town Square MCP server and it can scaffold the first one with you. Most first creations are one screen and take an evening.

townsquare mcp add russellville
  → connected as @kmcbride (verified)
Review queue, clear

The queue is clear.

Last review was Tuesday at 9:12 a.m. Three creations approved, one sent back with notes about the storage permission it asked for.

The cleared queue is the one empty that swaps the accent to sage. Every other mark in the system uses terracotta, because every other empty is neutral or an invitation. An empty moderation queue is the only one where "there is nothing here" is the outcome the committee was working toward, so the accent says done rather than pending. That is the whole exception, and it does not spread.

Marks for empties CSS only, ink plus one accent, drawn with a pen not a mascot

Rules that keep these from becoming an illustration library. Three shapes maximum per mark, since each is the element and its two pseudo elements. Strokes are 1.5px, the same weight as an icon, so a mark next to a chip does not look like a different product. Ink at 30 percent carries the form, one terracotta stroke carries the meaning, and nothing is filled except a 10 percent leaf. Each sits at a small off-axis rotation, between 2 and 5 degrees, which is the whole difference between "drawn" and "an image that failed to load".

Inline field error message under the field, icon plus text, never colour alone and never a tooltip

Validate on blur, clear on input, never validate while a finger is still typing. The error border is 1.5px terracotta so it is visible against the 1px hairline of a resting field without a colour comparison, and the message is always a sentence that names the actual cause. "Invalid handle" tells a resident nothing. "@kmcbride signed up in March" tells them to pick something else and why. Errors are wired with aria-invalid plus aria-describedby, so a screen reader hears the cause when focus lands, not a beep.

Failed action, with retry the work the resident did is still on screen; that is the promise, not the retry button
Before
Anyone know if the Prairie Creek ramp is open after the rain? Headed out Saturday.
Posting as @kmcbride
Sending
Anyone know if the Prairie Creek ramp is open after the rain? Headed out Saturday.
Posting as @kmcbride
Failed
Anyone know if the Prairie Creek ramp is open after the rain? Headed out Saturday.
That didn't send. Your post is still here, nothing was lost.

A failed action never clears the input, and it never shows a toast. A toast is for something that happened elsewhere; this happened right here, in the thing the resident is looking at, and it needs a decision from them. The first sentence is the fact, the second sentence is the reassurance, and "Save as draft" exists because the third try sometimes fails too and a person should be able to walk away without losing eighty words.

Reconnection

Reconnecting is a toast, going offline is a banner. Losing signal changes what the whole screen means and has to stay visible; getting it back is one moment and then it is over.

What survives offline is a design decision, not a caching accident. Today's front page, the last two hundred stories, every saved item, and the full directory including phone numbers and hours, because that is what you need when you are parked outside a shop that might be closed. Creations never cache: they are sandboxed third-party code and a stale copy of somebody else's app is a support problem nobody in this town signed up for. The bar states the time of the copy, never just the word "offline".

Stale data when a scrape fails the API serves the last good screen, so this timestamp is the only thing telling the truth
Fresh, under two hours

Updated 6 minutes ago

ink45, no dot, no colour. Present on every screen but never asking for attention.

A few hours

Updated at 7:12 this morning

Switches from relative to clock time, because "9 hours ago" makes a person do arithmetic. Ink60 and a small dot.

Over a day

Updated yesterday at 6:40 p.m.

Terracotta and a filled dot. The day word is doing the work; the colour is confirmation, not the message.

Some of this is a day old.

The Courier's feed stopped answering at 6:40 p.m. yesterday. Everything below is the last thing we got from it. Events and the directory are current.

0 to 2hrelative, ink45, no banner
2 to 18hclock time, ink60, hollow dot, no banner
18h+day plus clock, terracotta, filled dot, banner appears
72h+banner names the source and links the status page

The threshold is 18 hours and it is not arbitrary. The Courier posts in the morning; the city posts agendas in the evening. Anything under 18 hours means at most one publishing cycle was missed, which happens on a normal Sunday and is not worth a banner. Past 18 hours a resident is looking at a screen that could be wrong about a road closure, and the product has to say so before they act on it. The banner appears once, at the top of the affected section only, and it is scoped: it never claims the whole app is stale when only one feed is.

The timestamp is never hidden and never abbreviated away. This is the single line standing between "the app is quietly serving you Tuesday" and a resident driving to a meeting that was cancelled. Removing it to clean up a layout is the one change in this system that would be a genuine failure.

Skeletons, per surface its only job is to hold the exact shape the real thing will take, so nothing jumps
Today – loading
Story list

Row two has no thumbnail, because roughly half the town's stories do not carry a photo. A skeleton that always draws a thumb teaches a layout that will not arrive.

Directory grid
A creation booting
Ramp Conditions by @jhollis · reviewed July 28

Starting the sandbox

Runs isolated. It can see your handle and that you're verified, nothing else.

We already know the name, the builder, and the review date from the manifest, so the boot state shows them. A grey box would be throwing away information we are holding.

Skeletons are measured against the real component, not drawn by eye. Every block here matches its live counterpart's height and rhythm, including the 14px baseline of a headline line and the 64px thumbnail. If the page shifts when content lands, the skeleton failed and it would have been more honest to show nothing. Shimmer runs at 1400ms linear, one direction, and it stops entirely under reduced motion, leaving a flat 7 percent ink fill that still reads as pending.

Toasts, four semantics a toast is for something that already happened somewhere you are not looking
Saved to your list.
Ramp Conditions is live in the gallery.
Two of your listing photos were over 8 MB and were skipped.
Couldn't remove that bookmark.
Toast behaviour, live stacking, timing, and undo, because a toast you cannot catch is worse than no toast

Toasts land here, bottom left, above the tab bar.

Timing
ToastDismissWhy
info, no action4sConfirming a tap the finger already knows about.
info or good, with undo8sLong enough to read it, notice the mistake, and reach the button.
warn10sSomething did not happen the way it was asked. That earns a second look.
problemneverIt needs a decision. It waits for dismiss or retry.
Stacking
  • Three at once, maximum. The fourth pushes the oldest out early.
  • Newest enters at the bottom, older ones rise. The eye is already at the bottom of a phone.
  • Identical toasts collapse and count up rather than repeat: "3 stories saved."
  • Hovering or focusing anything in the stack pauses every timer in it.
  • A problem toast never auto-dismisses, and never gets pushed out by a newer one.

When a banner is right and a toast is wrong. A toast is an event: it happened, it is over, it will leave. A banner is a condition: it is true right now and it stays true whether or not you look at it. Offline is a condition. Stale data is a condition. A feed being down is a condition. All three are banners. Saving a bookmark, publishing a creation, and a failed photo upload are events, so they are toasts. The test is simple: if the statement is still true in thirty seconds, a toast is the wrong shape, because in thirty seconds the toast is gone and the truth is not.

Modals and sheets interrupting a person is expensive, so each one has to be a question only they can answer
Confirm

Leave without posting?

Your draft about the Prairie Creek ramp will be saved and it'll be here when you come back.

Destructive confirm

Remove the listing for River Valley Bicycles?

This can't be undone. The hours, the phone number, and the eleven photos go with it, and adding it back means starting from an empty form.

The destructive button is a terracotta outline, not a brick fill. Two reasons, and both matter. First, brick is the flood register and spending it on a delete button is how it stops meaning anything. Second, a filled button is the easy target, and the easy target on this dialog should be "Keep it". The outline makes the destructive choice deliberate to hit without hiding it, and the sentence above it does the actual work: it names what is lost, counts it, and says what recovery would cost. A dialog that only says "Are you sure?" has asked a resident to guess.

Informational sheet, live

What verified means here

Ten neighbours have said they know you're a real person in Russellville. That's the whole mechanism.

Town Square never stores your address, and verified is not the same as identified. A creation you open can see two things about you: your handle, and whether you're verified. Not your name, not your email, not where you are.

  • Vouches are private. You can see your count, not who vouched.
  • You can withdraw a vouch you gave, any time.
  • Unverified residents can read everything. Verified adds posting and building.
Focus and dismissal rules
  • On open, focus moves to the dialog's heading, not to a button. Landing on "Remove listing" is how an accident happens.
  • Tab is trapped between the first and last focusable element inside. Shift+Tab from the first wraps to the last.
  • Escape closes a confirm, an info sheet, and any non-destructive dialog.
  • Escape also closes a destructive confirm. It is the cancel path, and cancel is always safe.
  • Tapping the scrim closes an info sheet. It does not close either confirm, because a stray thumb on a phone should not answer a question for you.
  • On close, focus returns to the control that opened it, every time.
  • The page behind gets inert and stops scrolling. Background scroll under a sheet is the most common way this pattern breaks.
  • Sheets rise from the bottom on a phone and become a centred dialog at 640px and up. Same markup, one media query.
  • One layer at a time. A dialog never opens another dialog; it replaces itself.

Optimistic, but honest about it. The count moves the instant the finger lifts, because waiting 800ms to see a number change makes an app feel broken. The word "sending" and a soft pulse carry the pending state, and both go away together. A rollback puts the number back and raises a toast in the same frame, because a number quietly changing back is the single most disorienting thing an interface can do. Motion alone never carries this: the pulse is decoration, the word is the state.

Auto-load stops after five screens

Why they differ. In the directory a resident is hunting: they need to know how many are left, they need the footer, and they need to be able to leave and come back to the same place. Infinite scroll destroys all three. In the feed they are browsing, and a button between them and the next story is friction with nothing on the other side of it. Infinite scroll gets a floor anyway: after five screens it stops and asks, because a list with no bottom on a phone means the tab bar and the footer are unreachable, and because five screens is well past the point where somebody is still reading. Both endings are written, never a spinner that quietly stops spinning.

Motion specification every motion in the product, what it costs, and the sentence it is saying
MotionWhereDurationEasingWhat it communicatesReduced motion
Press responseEvery button, chip, card--ts-dur-1 90ms--ts-easeThe tap registered, before the network knows anything.Kept. Opacity only, no scale.
Focus ringEvery focusable0msnoneYou are here. Instantly.Unchanged. Focus never animates.
Enter, single elementToast, banner, inline error--ts-dur-3 260ms--ts-ease-outSomething arrived that you did not ask to see.Fade only, 90ms, no travel.
ExitToast, banner--ts-dur-2 160ms--ts-easeIt is leaving. Do not chase it.Instant removal.
Sheet riseBottom sheet--ts-dur-4 420ms--ts-ease-outA layer came up over the page, and the page is still under it.Fade in, 120ms. No travel.
Sheet dismissBottom sheet--ts-dur-3 260ms--ts-easeYou are being put back where you were.Instant.
Modal enterCentred dialog--ts-dur-2 160ms--ts-ease-outThis interrupted you on purpose.Fade only, no scale.
ScrimBehind any overlay--ts-dur-3 260ms--ts-easeThe page behind is not available right now.Kept. Opacity is not vestibular.
List staggerFeed, search results--ts-dur-3, 40ms apart, capped at 6--ts-ease-outThese arrived together, and in this order.Off. All items appear at once.
Page transitionTab and route change--ts-dur-2 160ms--ts-easeYou moved. You did not reload.Cross-fade, 90ms.
ExpandHours, story body, filters--ts-dur-3 260ms--ts-easeThis grew out of the thing you tapped.Snap open. Height is not animated.
Skeleton shimmerEvery skeleton1400ms looplinearThe app is working, not frozen.Off. Flat fill holds the shape.
Pending pulseOptimistic updates1200ms loop--ts-easeSent, not confirmed.Off. The word "sending" already says it.
RollbackOptimistic failure--ts-dur-2 160ms--ts-easeThat did not stick. Here is where things actually are.Instant, with the toast.
Stale banner dropTop of a section--ts-dur-3 260ms--ts-ease-outThis was not here a second ago. Read it.Appears without travel.
Progress fillDeterminate bar--ts-dur-4 420ms--ts-easeMeasured, not guessed.Kept. The bar is the information.
Indeterminate runUnknown duration1600ms loop--ts-easeStill working. No idea how long.Becomes a static striped bar plus text.

The rule that governs the whole table: motion is never the only carrier of a state change. Every row above has a non-motion partner. The pending pulse is paired with the word "sending". The stale banner is paired with a timestamp that changed colour and wording. The skeleton shimmer is paired with a fill that is visible when it is stopped. Turn every animation in this product off and nothing becomes unknowable, which is the only test that matters, because for some residents it is off already.

Motion, live the same six motions with reduced motion on and off, side by side

Reduced motion is not "everything off". Opacity and colour changes stay, because they are not vestibular and turning them off removes information. What goes is travel, scale, and anything looping: the sheet appears rather than rises, the stagger becomes simultaneous, the shimmer and the pending pulse stop. The press response survives as an opacity change, because losing the feedback that a tap landed is a worse outcome than the motion was.

Focus on every primitive one ring, two rings of offset, legible on cream, on white, and on navy
Quorum court sends the culvert back The Courier · 6:41 a.m.
Tonight at the Center for the Arts 7:30 p.m.

The ring's inner band is cream on light surfaces and navy-dark on the dark card, so there is always a gap between the control and the terracotta. Without it the ring blends into whatever it is sitting on.

Focus is visible for everyone, not only for keyboard users. These specimens render the ring permanently so it can be reviewed; in the product it is :focus-visible, so a mouse click does not leave a ring behind but a Tab key always does. The ring is 2px terracotta with a 2px offset band, drawn as a box-shadow so it never changes layout, and it is never removed, never replaced with a colour change, and never animated. Hit targets are 44px minimum even where the visible control is smaller: the toast dismiss is a 16px glyph in a 44px button.

Live regions and announcements polite for nearly everything, assertive exactly once, because a region that always shouts is a region people turn off

What gets announced
EventPolitenessAnnounced text
Toast, any kindpoliteThe toast line, without the word "toast" and without the icon.
Failed submissionassertiveThe failure, then the reassurance that the draft survived.
Crossing 18 hours stalepoliteThe banner text, once. Never repeated on re-render.

Optimistic pendingoffOnly the outcome is announced. Confirmed says nothing, rolled back announces politely.
  • Skeletons are aria-hidden="true" and the container is aria-busy="true". A screen reader reading forty empty boxes is a worse loading state than silence.
  • Live regions exist in the DOM before the text goes in them. A region created at the same moment as its message announces nothing.
  • Errors on a form are announced by focus moving to the first bad field, not by a live region. Two announcements for one problem is one too many.

The theming seam, and the system as a system

Every colour, space and radius in this sheet is a --ts-* custom property, and the same properties are injected into every sandboxed creation. That one decision means a town that reskins Town Square reskins every resident-built app inside it, without a single creation being edited or even reloaded. This section proves that, then writes down the rules that keep it true.

The three screens above are the same HTML, character for character, including the town name in the lockup. Nothing was copied and recoloured. Delta and Harbor each set a handful of custom properties on an ancestor and the whole surface follows, down to the shadow under the featured card, because the shadow is --ts-ink08 and not a hand-picked grey. The featured creation in each phone is the part that matters: in production that card is a sandboxed iframe built by a resident who has never heard of Harbor, and it reskins anyway.

What moved, and what did not Fifteen values in Delta, fourteen in Harbor. Zero names, zero components, zero creations.

Names are contract, values are not A resident ships a creation and moves on. The contract has to hold without them.
Adding is always safe

A new token nobody references yet cannot break anything. Ship it, document it, let components adopt it when they need it.

+ --ts-action: var(--ts-terracotta);
Changing a value is routine

This is the whole point of the seam. A town moves --ts-terracotta from clay to slate blue and every creation that styled a button with it moves too.

- --ts-terracotta: #C4714E;
+ --ts-terracotta: #3D7D8C;
Renaming is an SDK 1 break

Every creation using the old name silently falls back to whatever the browser default is, and the resident who built it in March is not coming back to fix it.

- --ts-terracotta: #C4714E;
+ --ts-accent-primary: #C4714E;
Removing is the same break, quieter

Nothing throws. The creation just renders with unstyled colour and looks abandoned, which is worse than an error because nobody gets told.

- --ts-terracotta14: rgba(196,113,78,0.14);
The list is pinned in a test, and the pinning is the contract. packages/tokens/src/index.test.ts asserts that twenty-six named variables still resolve. It does not assert a single value. Breaking the contract therefore requires editing that list on purpose, in a diff a reviewer can see, rather than by renaming a field in an object.
The reskin recipe Seven values carry an identity. Everything else is the product, and forking it is how you lose the product.
towns/harbor/theme.css
[data-town='harbor'] {
  /* 1. the structural colour: nav, dark cards, links */
  --ts-navy: #1F3B57;
  --ts-navy-dark: #17304A;
  /* 2. the action colour, and its pressed state */
  --ts-terracotta: #3D7D8C;
  --ts-terracotta-hover: #316875;
  /* 3. the tint that action colour sits on */
  --ts-terracotta-tint: #EAF5F7;
  /* 4. the screen. Keep it warm or keep it cool, commit either way */
  --ts-cream: #F4F6F6;
  /* 5. civic gold, for notices */
  --ts-gold: #D9A441;
  /* 6. sage, for open and verified */
  --ts-sage: #46736A;
  /* 7. optional: the editorial face */
  --ts-font-serif: 'Source Serif 4', Georgia, serif;
}
towns/harbor/town.json
{
  "name": "Town Square",
  /* the lockup's second line, and the only copy you must change */
  "place": "Rockland, Maine",
  "timezone": "America/New_York"
}
Do not touch
  • --ts-ink* and --ts-hairline. They are tuned for reading and they are why the type holds up at 4.4:1 in every town.
  • --ts-brick. One alarm register, shared across every town, so an emergency looks like an emergency to someone who moved here from Delta.
  • --ts-space-* and --ts-radius-*. Change these and creations built elsewhere stop lining up with your shell.
  • Component CSS. If you are editing a component to reskin, the reskin is wrong.
Your town in ten minutes
  1. 0:00 Fork the repo. Copy towns/harbor/ to towns/<yours>/.
  2. 1:00 Pick two colours you already own: one structural, one action. Paste them into --ts-navy and --ts-terracotta.
  3. 3:00 Run npm run tokens:check. It derives the alphas, the hover and the tint for you and reports every contrast pair.
  4. 5:00 Fix whatever it flagged. Usually this is darkening the action colour by one step.
  5. 7:00 Set place in town.json.
  6. 8:00 Open the sheet with ?town=<yours> and read the three screens above in your own palette.
  7. 10:00 Ship. No creation was touched, and no creation needs to be.

The recipe is short on purpose. A theming system that takes a week is a theming system nobody uses, and a town that cannot reskin in an afternoon will fork the components instead, which is the one outcome that kills the seam. The cost of that shortness is that some things are simply not themeable, and saying so plainly up front is kinder than letting a town discover it after they have already shipped.

Where a token is allowed to be wrong The seam does not check taste. It has to check contrast, because a bad value ships to every creation too.

Why this must run at build and not in review. The failing value does not stay in the shell. It is injected into every sandboxed creation on the next page load, so a town can break fifty apps it did not write and never see it, because the reviewer only ever looks at the shell.
The honest limits of the seam
  • Contrast is checkable, harmony is not. A town can pass every ratio and still look like a parking ticket. The tool says readable, not good.
  • A creation can hardcode. Nothing stops a builder writing #C4714E in their own CSS, and that creation will look wrong in Harbor forever. The MCP submission lints for hex literals and warns, it does not reject, because rejecting a working app over a colour is worse.
  • Photography does not theme. Every lead image in the three screens above is the same photograph. A cool-blue town running warm-golden local photos is a mismatch no token can fix.
  • Semantic drift. If a town sets --ts-sage to a red, every verified badge in every creation turns red and still means verified. The name survives, the meaning does not.
Semantic tokens, the layer this system is missing A component that asks for terracotta when it means "primary action" is describing a colour, not a role.

Today a button reaches for --ts-terracotta and a notice reaches for --ts-gold. That works while the palette and the roles line up, and it stops working the moment they do not. Harbor's action colour is a teal. It is still called terracotta in every creation in that town, and a builder reading the token list has to know the lore to understand why.

The fix is an alias layer on top of the raw palette. Raw tokens stay exactly as they are, keep their names, and keep resolving. Semantic tokens are added beside them and components migrate one at a time.

Proposed additions. Every one is a pure alias on day one, so the visual diff is zero.
SemanticResolves toMeans
--ts-actionvar(--ts-terracotta)the one thing on this screen a finger is meant to press
--ts-action-hovervar(--ts-terracotta-hover)pressed and hovered states of the above
--ts-action-quietvar(--ts-terracotta14)the wash behind a selected chip or an active tab
--ts-civicvar(--ts-gold)the town speaking: notices, closures, official postings
--ts-civic-textvar(--ts-gold-text)civic copy that has to pass on a light wash
--ts-verifiedvar(--ts-sage)vouched, open, alive. Never a brand accent
--ts-alarmvar(--ts-brick)an actual emergency. Not a validation error
--ts-quietvar(--ts-ink60)text that recedes: bylines, counts, timestamps
--ts-structurevar(--ts-navy)chrome, dark cards, the frame around the town
Written against raw tokens
.submit {
  background: var(--ts-terracotta);
  color: var(--ts-surface);
}
.notice { border-left: 3px solid var(--ts-gold); }
.badge  { color: var(--ts-sage); }
Written against semantic tokens
.submit {
  background: var(--ts-action);
  color: var(--ts-surface);
}
.notice { border-left: 3px solid var(--ts-civic); }
.badge  { color: var(--ts-verified); }
Both render this, in every town
Weir Road closed Thursday
verified
The migration cost, stated honestly
Additive

Nine new names, zero renames, zero removals. The pinned test grows by nine lines and nothing in it changes. Every existing creation keeps working because every raw token keeps existing.

Two names for one colour

The real cost. For a while both --ts-terracotta and --ts-action are valid and a builder has to be told which to prefer. Documentation, not engineering, and it is a smaller tax than the lore tax we pay now.

Never a rename

Raw tokens are not deprecated and are not scheduled for removal. They are the physical palette and there are legitimate uses for reaching at it directly. Semantics are the layer above, not a replacement.

Where it pays

The day a town wants a different action colour from its structural colour, or a dark mode, or an accessible high-contrast variant. Every one of those is a role change, and roles are the thing we currently cannot express.

[data-density='compact'] {
  --ts-row-y:    var(--ts-space-2);  /* 16 -> 8 */
  --ts-row-gap:  var(--ts-space-2);  /* 12 -> 8 */
  --ts-row-lead: 32px;               /* 44 -> 32 */
  --ts-row-title: 15px;              /* 17 -> 15 */
}

The row component reads var(--ts-row-y, var(--ts-space-4)), so it works with no density set and gets denser when a container asks. Two consequences worth naming: the tap target still floors at 44px, so compact buys vertical space and never accessibility, and a creation inside a compact container inherits the density too, which is how a resident-built list stops looking foreign next to the directory.

[data-theme='dark'] {
  /* the surfaces get warmer as they get darker, not greyer */
  --ts-cream:   /* ink, pulled 7% toward terracotta */;
  --ts-surface: /* ink, pulled 14% toward terracotta */;
  --ts-stone:   /* ink, pulled 26% toward terracotta */;
  /* ink becomes light, and the muted rule inverts with it */
  --ts-ink:     /* cream, warmed 8% toward gold */;
  --ts-ink60:   /* cream at 62% */;
  --ts-hairline:/* cream at 13% */;
  /* accents lift, because the same hue at the same weight
     loses roughly two stops of apparent contrast on dark */
  --ts-terracotta: /* terracotta, 24% toward cream */;
  --ts-sage:       var(--ts-sage-light);
}
Recommendation: do not ship this yet
  1. The one-dark-card rule collapses. Restraint in this product is expressed by having exactly one dark card per screen. On a dark screen that card has nothing to be darker than, so the featured creation and the navy nav stop being emphasis and become texture. That is not a colour problem, it is a hierarchy problem, and it needs a second emphasis mechanism designed before dark mode is worth having.
  2. Two of the five hues stop working. Gold at 14 percent alpha on a dark surface is a smudge, and brick on dark loses the alarm quality that is the entire reason brick exists. Both need dark-specific values, which means the override is not seven lines, it is closer to thirty.
  3. It doubles the reskin surface. Every town now has to pass the contrast check twice, and a town that only tests light will ship a broken dark mode to every creation in it.
  4. What would change the answer. Real demand. Town Square is read in the morning and at lunch far more than at midnight, and there is no evidence yet that residents want it. If it does become a request, ship it as a town-level opt-in with its own contrast gate, never as a system preference we follow silently, because a town that has not tested dark should not be handed one.
Accessibility, as a property of the token set Checked once for all three towns, so a reskin that fails is visible before it ships.
Contrast ratios, computed from the shipped values. Green passes AA at its size, amber is large-text only, red fails.

The two amber rows are load bearing. River Valley's terracotta is 3.34 on cream and 3.61 under white. It is approved for a button label at 17px semibold and for a 15px or larger link, and it is not approved for 13px caption copy. Delta and Harbor both clear 4.5 and could take it anywhere, which is exactly the kind of thing a town gets wrong when it assumes the default palette is the strict one.
Gold is never text. 1.85 in River Valley. That is why --ts-gold-text exists as a separate token at 4.92, and why the notice component fills with --ts-gold14 and sets its copy in --ts-gold-text rather than doing the obvious thing.
ink45 is a boundary, not a colour. 2.83 means dots, dividers, and disabled glyphs that are never the only way to read a state. Any run of ink45 that a resident has to read is a bug.
Targets. 44px minimum on every pressable thing, including in compact density where the visible row is 36px and the target bleeds past it. Chips grow a transparent hit area rather than growing visually.

Hand-rolled spacing

On the 4px scale
.card  { padding: var(--ts-space-4); }

Every gap is a multiple of four, so anything built by anyone lines up with anything else. This is what makes fifty creations feel like one town.

Naming rules
  • Every published property starts --ts-. That prefix is the namespace a creation trusts, and nothing else may use it.
  • Kebab case, derived mechanically from the source object. terracottaHover becomes --ts-terracotta-hover.
  • A trailing number is an alpha percentage of the hue named before it: --ts-navy60 is navy at 60 percent.
  • Names describe the palette, not the layout. There is no --ts-card-padding, because padding belongs to a component and the component belongs to the shell.
The three breaking changes
  1. Renaming a token. Every creation using the old name loses its styling silently.
  2. Removing a token. Same failure, and no error is raised anywhere.
  3. Changing what a token means. The name still resolves, so nothing breaks visually, and every creation now says something false. Making --ts-sage a warning colour is worse than deleting it.

Everything else, including every value in every town, is routine. If you are unsure which side of the line you are on, the test at packages/tokens/src/index.test.ts is the answer: if your change edits that list, it is breaking.

The reason to be this strict about a colour list is that Town Square's value compounds with builders, not readers. A resident who ships a lake-level app in March is not on call. If a rename in June breaks it, nobody fixes it, the app quietly rots, and the next resident sees a graveyard and decides not to bother. The token contract is not a styling convenience, it is the promise that makes building here worth a Saturday.

12

Contribution, and the composer

Everything a resident puts into Town Square is a typed record with a shape and a purpose: an event, a correction to a listing, a notice from an organisation, a collection, a photo of something that happened. There is no box that says "what's on your mind". Every record is versioned, attributed and revertible, which is what makes light moderation survivable in a town this size.

Entry point, one plus and a typed chooser Choosing the shape first is what stops this becoming a complaint board. The choice is five nouns, not a blank field.

There is no general post box here, on purpose. Why

The plus, three states

What each type becomes
Chooser rowRecord typeGoes live
An eventeventImmediately, verified residents
A correctionbusiness v+1After owner or moderator sees it
A noticenoticeImmediately, urgent is reviewed
A collectioncollectionImmediately
A photophotoImmediately
Typed beats freeform because the type is the moderation policy. A general status box has no shape, so it accepts everything, and the thing it accepts most easily is a grievance about a neighbour. Nobody sets out to build a complaint board. You build a box, and the box decides. Asking for the shape first does three useful things at once: it turns "someone should do something about the potholes on Weir Road" into either an event, a correction or nothing, it gives every record fields that make it findable in six months, and it means the rules can be per type rather than one global standard nobody agrees on. Corrections are checked against the listing they touch. Notices are gated on being an organisation. Photos allow no comments. None of that is possible when everything arrives as untyped text. The cost is real: a resident with something to say that fits no shape is turned away. We take that cost knowingly, and the chooser says so in plain words rather than hiding it.

  1. Header names the thing being made. "Adding an event", never "New item". If a resident cannot say what they are making, the composer has already failed.
  2. Autosave indicator, not a save button. Three states: Saving, Saved, Saved offline, will sync. It is a status line with role="status" so it is announced once, not on every keystroke.
  3. Write and Preview, never side by side on a phone. 370px cannot hold both honestly. Preview renders the record exactly as the town will see it, including the attribution line.
  4. The body is the only part that changes per type. Everything above and below is identical across all five composers.
  5. Attribution is shown and locked. There is no author field anywhere in any composer. It is written from the session on the server.
  6. Publish bar sticks to the bottom. Secondary on the left, primary on the right, both 44px tall. The primary verb names the type: "Post event", "Send correction", "Publish notice".

Date parse confirmation, five states Never silently correct a human. Show the reading, offer the fix, and keep the words they typed visible above it.
Empty

The placeholder teaches the input by example. No format is documented anywhere.

Parsed, confident

We read that as Saturday 14 June, 7pm. Is that right?

Ambiguous

Two readings of that. Which one?

Nothing is picked for you. A market at 7am and a game at 7pm are both normal here.

Corrected by hand

You set this by hand. We stopped guessing.

Could not read

We could not find a date in that. Try a day and a time, or set it by hand.

The words you typed are kept. Nothing you wrote was thrown away.

The parse line is a question, not a result. A date picker is unambiguous and slow. Natural language is fast and occasionally wrong, and a wrong start time is the single most damaging error in this whole product: fifteen people stand in a car park at the wrong hour and nobody trusts the events feed again. So the input takes what someone would say out loud, then reads it back in full prose with the weekday spelled out, because "14/06" and "06/14" look identical to a person skimming and "Saturday 14 June" does not. The ambiguous state deliberately picks nothing. Defaulting to pm would be right most of the time in a town with evening ball games, and wrong every Saturday morning at the market, which is exactly the population that matters most.

Post a notice, and the gate in front of it The gate is a route, not a refusal. The severity list spells out the consequence of each level in the level's own words.
Notice – no permission yet
About Notices

Notices come from organisations

A notice goes out under an organisation's name, so residents know who is telling them. The library, a church, the school district, a city department. Your account is a person, so this one is not open to you yet.

If you run something in town, or you help run it, we can attach you to it. It takes a couple of days and a person reads it.

Or, if what you have is one of these

  • Something is happening. That is an event, and anyone verified can add one.
  • Something is wrong on a listing. That is a correction.
  • Water is out on your street right now. Ring the city. We are not an emergency service and we will not pretend to be.
Notice – verified organisation
Posting a notice as First United Methodist
Saved
Say it the way you would say it from the pulpit. 104 / 400
How far this goes

Supper time changing is a notice. Urgent is for when somebody could get hurt. Nobody thinks less of you for using the quiet one, and everyone notices the loud one twice.

When
Posting as First United Methodist Church, by @rev.tillman
The gate is written as a redirect because the person hitting it is almost always right and just in the wrong door. Somebody who wants to post a notice has something to tell the town. Refusing them and stopping there teaches them the product is closed. So the gate names the actual reason, offers the route that solves it, and then lists the three things they probably meant instead, in the order they are likely. The third one sends them to the phone, which is the correct answer and the one a community platform is usually too proud to give. On severity: the failure mode here is not malice, it is a kind secretary who genuinely believes the supper time matters urgently, and it does, to her. So the consequence is written in physical terms, "wakes up every phone in Russellville, tonight, including people asleep", rather than in policy terms. The date of the last real use is shown because it is the most persuasive sentence on the screen.

EXIF is the obvious leak, and telling people about it is the point. We built a whole identity model on never storing an address, and then the first photo somebody uploads from their front porch carries the coordinates of their front porch inside the file. Stripping it silently would be correct and invisible. Saying it out loud, in the composer, at the moment the photo lands, is correct and legible, and legibility is the thing that makes a stranger believe the rest of the privacy claims. "See what was removed" is there for the one resident in fifty who wants to check, and their checking is what makes the promise real for the other forty nine. The location field is a directory place and never a dropped pin, for the same reason: a pin can be a house, a listing cannot.

In the composer
Posting as @dana_h, verified resident

Not a dropdown, not editable, not hidden. Someone posting for two organisations switches account at the top of the app, not at the bottom of a form, so the choice is never made by accident in the last second before publishing.

Needs vouching

Saved, and it will post the moment you are verified. Adding events is for verified residents. You need ten neighbours to vouch, and you have four. We are holding this for you, nothing is lost.

Being read

A moderator has this. Urgent notices are read by a person before they send. Usually inside an hour during the day. If it is genuinely happening right now, ring the city at 479 968 2098 and do not wait on us.

Scheduled

Goes out Friday at 8am. Nobody can see it before then, including you on another device. You can change it or pull it back any time before it sends.

Live

It is up. 41 people have seen it. Editing it makes version 2, and the old one stays where it is.

Turned down

A moderator did not put this one up, and left you a note.

This one reads as a complaint about a specific neighbour rather than an event, and that is the one thing Town Square does not carry. If the clean up on Skyline Drive is actually happening on Saturday, put it back as an event with a time and I will approve it straight away. Ring me if that is not fair, my number is on the moderators page.

A moderator, Thursday

Nothing was deleted. The draft is exactly as you wrote it.

The rejection is the most important screen in this section. It is the only moment where the platform tells a resident no, and how it reads decides whether they ever contribute again. So it is a person writing to a person: it names what was wrong with the record and never with them, it says exactly what would make it acceptable, it commits to acting quickly if they do, and it gives them a way to argue including a phone number. It is signed "a moderator" rather than by name, because in a town of 29,000 a named moderator gets stopped in the Kroger car park, and that is how you lose your only moderator. The brick alarm colour is nowhere near this screen. Being turned down is not an emergency.
Version history, from the contributor's side A revert is a new version, not a deletion, so the history reads as a record of care rather than a disciplinary file.

Not this

Three untrue words. It was not rejected, it was superseded. It was not removed, it is version 3 and always will be. And there is no strike system, so the threat is a fiction that costs a real contributor.

Same facts, correct verbs, and it ends with the contributor's work winning. The revert is described as a scheduling problem, which is what it actually was.

Autosave, three states
Saving Saved Saved on this phone

The offline state is the honest one and it says where the copy actually is. Signal on the river road is bad enough that a composer which pretends to have saved is a composer that loses somebody's work.

Discard

Throw this draft away?

"Summer reading kickoff", with the time and place you already put in. This one is a real delete, not a version, because a draft was never published and there is nothing to keep a history of.

"Keep it" sits on the left and reads first, and it is the button a thumb finds. Discard is bordered rather than filled, because a filled destructive button is a button people press by accident.

Natural language date, resting and focused

Focus opens the quick days, which cover most of what gets added. "Pick a date" is the last chip and opens the native picker, because the fallback has to be the thing every phone already knows how to do.

Rate limiting, as a pause rather than a wall The most prolific contributor in town is an asset. Treat them like one, and say what the limit is actually protecting.
Friction – a busy afternoon
Hold on a second Nine today

That is nine things you have added today, and they were all good ones

Town Square puts a pause in after nine in a day. Not because you did anything wrong. It is there so that if somebody's account is ever taken over, the town does not wake up to two hundred fake events, and the pause has to apply to everyone or it protects nobody.

You can post again at 6pm, about two hours.
  • Keep writing. Drafts still save, there is no limit on those.
  • Corrections to listings still go through. Those are reviewed anyway.
  • Anything already scheduled still sends on time.

If you run the market or the school calendar and nine a day is genuinely not enough, say so and we will raise yours. That takes a message, not an application.

The ladder, in order
  1. 1
    Nothing at all, up to six a day. Most residents never see any of this, including the busy ones.
  2. 2
    A quiet line at seven. "Seventh one today." Sits under the publish bar. No confirmation, no delay.
  3. 3
    The pause at nine. The screen on the left. Drafting continues, publishing waits.
  4. 4
    A moderator is told at fifteen attempts. The resident is told they were told. A limit nobody is watching is a limit that only annoys honest people.
Seventh one today. No trouble, just so you know.

Step two is the one that does the real work. It makes a person notice their own volume without stopping them, and in testing that is usually enough.

The limit is explained by its threat model, not by its number. "You have reached your daily limit" is a sentence that makes a person feel suspected, and the person hitting it is nearly always the one running the market booth or the school calendar. So the copy names the actual thing being defended, a compromised account posting two hundred fake events overnight, and admits straight out that the rule has to apply to everyone or it defends nobody. It then lists what still works, because the most useful sentence in a rate limit screen is the one that says the work is not lost. And the escalation path is a message to a person, not a form, which is a thing you can only offer in a product built for one town.

This will be version 1. Anyone verified can correct it later, you will be told when they do, and you can put your version back.

The whole section is one argument: a record you can fix cheaply does not need to be policed expensively. Every design choice here leans on the same two lines in the data model. Because a version is never destroyed, a correction from a stranger is low stakes, so corrections can be open to any verified resident instead of to owners only. Because attribution is dual, a creation writing on a resident's behalf can be cut off without deleting the resident's work, so residents can safely let their apps write. Because revert is a forward operation, a moderator can undo something in one tap and the contributor can put it back, which is why the revert screen can be written kindly and mean it. Take versioning out and every one of those choices flips to the defensive version: locked fields, owner-only edits, a review queue in front of everything, and a product nobody bothers to contribute to.

The bottom of the phone already stacks the home indicator, the tab bar and the ask bar. We considered docking a fourth strip above them and chose not to: four layers of chrome reads as a control panel, and the design brief bans exactly that energy. So playback borrows the ask band. Ask never disappears, it folds to its sparkle and stays one tap away, and the whole band returns to it the moment audio stops. The scrub is the strip's own top edge, three pixels of terracotta that survive at a glance, and the title truncates rather than wrapping because the bar must never change height.

Same register as the dark mode note in section 11: considered and not chosen, so the next designer does not relitigate it from scratch. If a town ever runs without Ask, the swap degrades to the strip alone and nothing else moves.

The bar expands into a sheet and the sheet is deliberately underwhelming: cover, scrub, three transport controls, three quiet chips. No queue, no up next, no autoplay into a second episode. This is a town's podcast, not a retention surface, and the listener chose one episode, not a session. The skip buttons carry their numerals beside minted glyphs because fifteen back and thirty forward are conventions worth keeping, not branding worth redrawing.

Section 06 draws the seam and this specimen states the policy on top of it: the host offers the town's tokens inside the frame and does not enforce them. A builder who adopts them gets a native look for free; a brand like Eleva can bring its whole visual world instead, and the review committee judges it against the content guidelines, not against our palette. The specimen here is drawn with token mixes because this sheet cannot carry foreign CSS, which is itself the demonstration: only a real guest bundle can truly leave the system.

What holds is the chrome. Host bar, sandbox badge, attribution and the footer with Report belong to the shell in every skin, and the footer now names the gate: a custom look passed review, and the version of the guidelines it passed.
